REFERENCE TO REPORT IN WINNIPEG "FREE PRESS" OF JUNE 8
speechtext:
On a matter of privilege, Mr. Speaker, I have before me the Winnipeg Free Press of Thursday, June 8, in which there is an article headed: "The wheat agreement-Mr. Howe's explanations"; and the last paragraph of that article, in the third column, reads as follows:
It is a matter of record in and out of parliament that the Conservative and C.C.F. parties were just as blind as the Liberal party to the weakness of the wheat agreement. Both the Conservative and C.C.F. parties have voted for this agreement on every occasion when it has been put to the test. . . .
That is not true, Mr. Speaker. The United Kingdom-Canada wheat agreement as such has never been voted on in this House of Commons. The agreement was sanctioned by order in council, under extension of the War Measures Act, in July, 1946. As reported at page 4833 of Hansard of August 15, 1946, I said, with respect to the present Canadian-British wheat agreement: "I am absolutely opposed to it." I stated my reasons, and quoted a portion of the Winnipeg Free Press editorial of August 1, 1946. I trust that the Free Press will make the proper correction or explanation.

PERSONNEL DISCHARGED OR RELEASED
speechtext:
1.	In each department or branch of government or board or corporation set up by the government, how many employees, if any, have been discharged or been in any way released for reasons having to do with security?
2.	What was the effective date in each such case?
3.	What were the position and duties of each such employee at the time of his discharge or release?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: PERSONNEL DISCHARGED OR RELEASED
speechtext:
I think I should answer now this question of the hon. member for Kamloops, which had earlier been passed as an order for return but has now been restored to the order paper. The hon. me-'ber's question should be considered in relation to

Questions
two other sets of questions standing in his name on today's order paper as Nos. 9 and 10, as follows:
1.	In each department or branch of government or board or corporation set up by the government, on what date respectively was any security screening first completed?
2.	Are there any such departments, branches, boards or corporations where no such screening has taken place? If so, what were the reasons?
1.	What were the positions in the national research council held at the time of their discharge by the two employees who were discharged for security reasons in March of 1946?
2.	What was the nature of their respective duties in these positions?
These questions all have to do with what has been referred to as screening of civil service personnel for security reasons, and I think it is desirable that I should answer them orally, all at the same time, in the following terms:
Those who serve the state should be loyal to the state. The loyalty of civil servants is expected by the government of Canada as a routine condition precedent to their employment. The responsibility for ensuring that civil service employees are loyal rests upon the head of each department, or agency, usually the deputy minister. It also rests in part upon the civil service commission. The departmental head and the civil service commission is each expected to take such steps [DOT] as may be considered necessary to make sure that this responsibility is properly discharged.

subtopic: PERSONNEL DISCHARGED OR RELEASED
speechtext: All of them.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: PERSONNEL DISCHARGED OR RELEASED
speechtext:
To this end a minister or deputy minister, where he considers it necessary, may refer to the Royal Canadian Mounted Police for a report on any civil servant doing work in connection with which it is necessary that there should be no doubt whatever as to the civil servant's loyalty. When the names of such civil servants are referred to the Royal Canadian Mounted Police, a check is made and the information thereby secured is reported back to the deputy head of the department concerned. In this report the mounted police do not in any case express any opinion as to whether a given civil servant should be retained in employment, or should be discharged. They provide merely a factual report concerning the civil servant reported upon; and it is the head of the department who decides whether, upon the basis of the Royal Canadian Mounted Police report or otherwise, the civil servant in question should be retained in employment or discharged.
The standard by which the loyalty of a given civil servant is judged depends in an important measure upon the degree of trustworthiness which is required in the work
[Mr. GarsonJ
which he is doing. In some cases entire departments have been designated by the cabinet as vulnerable departments which require from the civil servants operating them a special degree of trustworthiness. In other cases sections or branches of departments dealing with secret matters have been declared as vulnerable. In still other cases, departments or branches of departments which had not been dealing with secret work previously are declared vulnerable upon being given secret work to do.
The civil servants employed in vulnerable branches or departments must have such a high degree of trustworthiness as to be beyond any doubt whatever. The government cannot wait for actual cases of espionage or sabotage or other offences to take place; the government cannot safely employ or continue to employ in secret or unusually confidential work persons about whose trustworthiness there is any doubt whatever. Thus, in considering the report from the Royal Canadian Mounted Police, and data from other sources, the head of a vulnerable department must resolve all doubts, even the slightest, in favour of the government. He should therefore refuse to continue in employment to do secret or confidential work any person concerning whom doubt exists.
This being so, it would be most unfair to the civil servant whose trustworthiness is perhaps no more than in some slight doubt that in addition to refusing to continue his employment, the government should, without proof, brand him as an untrustworthy person. The government considers that it would be quite unwarranted in taking any overt action which would injure such person's reputation or interfere with his chances of alternative employment in positions not of the same secret and confidential character.
The two employees of the national research council

and I am referring now to question No. 10 on today's order paper-who were discharged for security reasons in March of 1946, were two who, having been mentioned in the report of the royal commission on espionage, had been convicted of offences under the Official Secrets Act. Therefore the government had no objection to disclosing information concerning them in reply to a question by the hon. member for Kamloops on May 22, 1950, and will answer in due course the question No. 10 on today's order paper, in -the name of the hon. member for Kamloops.
In connection, however, with each of the other civil servants who have been released for security reasons, the government feels it would be unjust to disclose the information sought by the hon. member's question with regard to the date of discharge and the position and

duties of such civil servants at the time of their release. Such information would in almost all cases disclose their identity.
It will be seen, moreover, from the foregoing that the security responsibilities of the departmental head and of the civil service commission are such that the checking or screening of all government employees in the Canadian civil service, with or without the assistance of factual reports from the Royal Canadian Mounted Police, is a process which never ends and which, therefore, is never complete as of any certain date.

speechtext:
the second reading of Bill No. 268, to amend the Foreign Insurance Companies Act, 1932.
He said: As the house is already aware, this bill and the companion bill to amend the Canadian and British Insurance Companies Act were passed in the other place. Since the original insurance acts were passed in 1868 they have necessarily had to be revised from time to time, and the last substantial revision was in 1932. While there have been certain amendments made since that time, the acts have stood substantially unchanged.
Several desirable amendments have been accumulating for a good many years, including especially a revision of the investment provisions in order to bring them up to date. The purpose of this bill, and of the companion bill, is to bring the acts into closer conformity with current conditions and to remove certain anomalies in the treatment of Canadian companies as compared with the treatment of British and foreign companies.
The bills were prepared in collaboration with the superintendent of insurance, and it would be my intention after second reading is approved to have them referred to the banking and commerce committee in order that the clauses may be given detailed consideration and the superintendent of insurance may be available to explain the different provisions. I think I should say that there are no amendments of great moment; none that will arouse any particular controversy.
The investment provisions have been amended to bring these acts, as I have said, into line with modern conditions. I do not know that I need to go into the changes in detail. They include such things as authorizing investment in equipment trust certificates, which have become a common vehicle for railway financing. Provision is also made for investment in revenue producing real estate which is subject to lease-in other words, the lease option agreements with which hon. members of the house are familiar, and which have become extremely popular in recent years, both here and in the United States. Since it is a relatively new departure under the Insurance Act, the amount which can be invested under that category is limited to five per cent.
Then there are some changes in connection with the qualifications for investment in common shares. The criterion at present is
3472	HOUSE OF
Foreign Insurance Companies Act that investment may be made, within the limitation provided under the act, in the common shares of any corporation that has in each of the seven years preceding the date of investment paid dividends of at least four per cent of the par value, or $4 per share if the shares have no par value. It is proposed that in place of the $4 test for shares of no par value, the dividends in each of the seven years must have been equal to at least four per cent of the average value at which the shares were carried in the capital stock account of the corpora'.ion. That is an illustration of the type of change provided to bring the legislation in line with modern conditions.
The other important change in connection with the investment provisions is that what is known as the amortization principle will be allowed in connection with the bonds of the dominion, any province of Canada, the United Kingdom, or the United States of America. At the present time, as the house is aware, all insurance companies registered under the act are required to take their securities into account at market values in the annual statement deposited with the department. In practice, however, Canadian companies have been taking them into account at the market values or book values, whichever was lower, and since this is a conservative practice it has been encouraged. It is now proposed that life insurance companies be permitted to carry securities issued by the government of Canada or of any province of Canada, or of the United States or the United Kingdom, at values not exceeding the "amortized" values, that is, values calculated mathematically having regard to the purchase price, the actual interest payments, the date of maturity, and the amount to be received at maturity. I think that basis is used in almost all of the states of the United States.
Then there are other provisions, such as a clause which would permit a company to reduce the par value of the shares below $100 if desired. The house will recall that in the last revision of the Bank Act an amendment was introduced permitting the shares of banks to be reduced to not less than $10. There will be a similar provision in the insurance companies act.
There are a number of other provisions of perhaps no general significance. They are technical in some cases, although important for the efficient administration of these companies.
As I say, the bill will be referred to the standing committee on banking and commerce, and in that committee detailed consideration can be given to the provisions to which I have referred.

speechtext:
Right Hon. C. D. Howe (Minister of Trade
and Commerce) moved that the house go into committee to consider the following resolution:
That it is expedient to present a bill, cited as the Defence Supplies Act, to empower the Minister of Trade and Commerce to buy or otherwise acquire and deal with defence supplies: construct or otherwise acquire, projects: acquire, store and otherwise deal with material entering into the manufacture of defence supplies or the development, repair or maintenance of projects; arrange for the performance of commercial and professional services; require priority in delivery or construction and to

require persons who have received offers, fair and reasonable in his opinion, for supplies, projects or services to meet the requirements subject to an appeal to the exchequer court on the question of price; also to empower the minister to buy or otherwise acquire defence supplies and construct or carry out projects required by the Department of National Defence; also to empower the governor in council to appoint assistants to the minister and advisers and advisory boards and to fix their remuneration and expenses; with provision also for the approval by the governor in council of contracts except in emergent cases and where the sum involved does not exceed a certain specified amount.
He said: Mr. Speaker, the defence supplies bill to be based on this resolution will make new provision for the procurement of munitions and defence supplies. At present provision for procurement is made in the Department of Munitions and Supply Act, 1939, as amended to date. The existing statute was drafted at the outbreak of war, and revised in the light of experience and to meet changing war conditions. It well served its purpose, both during the war and after. It was, however, designed primarily to deal with a state of war and with the aftermath of war. We consider that the time is fitting to replace it with legislation which will be more closely suited to the conditions of the day.
Clearly this is no time to take any action that would hamper the defence of the country; for we are not free from the threat of aggression. Indeed we must devote much of our energies and our resources to deterring aggression. We must strengthen ourselves so we may be able to resist the aggressor and overcome him if we fail to deter him. Hence we have endeavoured to frame the legislation so that we shall not lessen our ability to provide for the needs of defence. We have aimed at retaining such powers, and no others, as will under present conditions safeguard the interests of defence in the field of procurement of supplies.
The bill grants the minister the general authority to procure defence supplies, to stockpile strategic materials, to construct defence projects, and to let contracts for shipbuilding and ship repairing for government departments. We consider that it is highly desirable to continue to vest in the minister the procurement authority for the requirements of the armed services. Our experience has shown that the method which we have adopted of centralizing defence purchasing in civilian hands is efficient and economical.
During the war we developed in the department of munitions and supply one of the best methods of procurement of any of the allied nations. We built up an extremely efficient civilian purchasing agency for the services. Many of the key personnel involved in these activities during the war
Defence Supplies
carried on as employees of the Canadian Commercial Corporation, and we have been able to secure in peacetime much of the efficiency, economy of effort and concentration of purpose that we secured during the war. In the last fiscal year, the Canadian Commercial Corporation made purchases of over $200 million for the services, at a cost of less than one-half of one per cent.
The minister is also given the powers which may be necessary to enable defence contracts to be completed. I well realize how greatly we can rely on our own people and how little we need rely on mandatory powers. I have had a good deal to do in the past years with the industrial aspects of war and defence. Some of those years have been bitter and trying, but throughout them all we have been heartened by the ready co-operation that every section of Canada and every sector of Canadian life have given to the tasks that faced us. Nevertheless, even with the best good will and co-operation on all sides, circumstances may still arise where some mandatory powers are needed. A supplier may be unable to meet an essential defence need because of prior commitments at home or abroad. A contractor may be unable to make delivery, on schedule, of defence supplies because of conflicting requirements, domestic or foreign. Hence the bill grants the minister power to obtain a priority for defence contracts over other contracts, and power to ensure the delivery of materials essential to the production of defence supplies and to the completion of defence projects.
Before the minister enters into a contract, the approval of the governor in council must be obtained, except:
(a)	where in the minister's opinion the contract must be executed immediately in the interests of defence;
(b)	where the estimated expenditure does not exceed $15,000;
(c)	where the estimated expenditure does
not exceed $50,000 in cases where competitive tenders have been obtained and the lowest tender accepted.	.
The minister, however, shall report to the governor in council contracts involving more than $5,000 which have been entered into without the latter's approval.
The minister is granted authority to enter into contracts without calling for tenders as required under section 36 of the Publio Works Act in four cases:
(1)	Where the disclosure of the specifications would, in the opinion of the minister or of the Minister of National Defence, be prejudicial to the interests of defence.

Defence Supplies
(2)	Where the supplies are to be acquired from, or the project executed by, a crown company. This provision is intended to extend to crown companies an exception already contained in the Public Works Act for works to be executed by government employees.
(3)	Where the contract covers ships or ship repairs.
I shall deal for a moment with the special provisions relating to ships. The bill gives the minister authority to place contracts for shipbuilding and repairs to meet the requirements of the Department of National Defence and of other government departments. He is authorized to let such contracts to any shipyard specified by the governor in council. The purpose of these provisions for allocation is to ensure the continuance of shipbuilding facilities in Canada adequate to the needs of defence. In the last war tremendous demands were made on Canadian shipyards, and they met their task magnificently. If there should be another war, we can be sure that they would be again called upon to make a great contribution. Although we have undertaken what is an extensive shipbuilding program for defence, it does not utilize the full capacities of our yards. We consider it is therefore desirable that such shipbuilding as we are undertaking be allocated with the object of sustaining in Canada a nucleus of facilities strategically located. The bulk of such contracts would be placed to meet the requirements of the Department of National Defence.
There is in addition a comparatively small amount of shipbuilding for other departments, such as the Department of Public Works and the Department of Transport. It is considered practical that the minister be given authority to place such contracts so that the full benefit of allocation may be obtained. We intend to consult the Canadian maritime commission and to obtain the advice of the commission as to the yards in which contracts should be placed to best further our general objective.
The fourth case in which the provisions of the Public Works Act would not apply is when in the opinion of the governor in council the contracts should in the public interest be exempt from that act. This provision is designed to meet the situation that can arise in our defence works in remote areas. A contract is let to a contractor for works in the north. While he is at work new factors may enter into our defence planning. As a result we may find we need more buildings than we contracted for. The practical course is to come to terms with the contractor already at work and on location. Or again we may need to place a contract for a project which calls for very highly specialized technical
IMr. Howe.]
knowledge where we have no choice of contractors. We would be able to cover these cases under this provision after the approval of the governor in council had been obtained.
Hon. members may be interested in a brief comparison between some of the main features of the bill and of the existing authority, the Department of Munitions and Supply Act.
The proposed bill relates to the same defence field as the present act; the definition of defence supplies is what is defined in the present act as "munitions of war" and "supplies". "Project" has the same meaning in the bill as in the act.
The provision which gives the minister the exclusive authority to procure for the Department of National Defence corresponds with the provisions in the present act.
The minister's powers respecting production and the delivery of supplies are a curtailment of his powers in the act. The power to compel manufacture of supplies or the construction of projects has been removed.
The bill does not grant the minister the authority to mobilize, control, and regulate any branch of trade or industry; or to issue orders, permits and licences; or the authority to do such things as the minister deems incidental to or expedient for the exercise of any of his powers.
The provision has been dropped which permitted the minister to exercise his powers without restriction or limitation by any other legislation. In the proposed bill the specific cases in which it is intended existing legislation should not restrict or limit him are set out.
The mandatory powers-that is, those dealing with priority and with delivery of supplies-are a considerable curtailment of the present powers in the act. The priority authority is effective only in respect of persons who actually contract to deliver defence supplies or to construct projects, and the powers relating to the delivery of supplies are effective only in respect of persons in the business of dealing in materials used for defence supplies or projects. There is a difference, too, in the terms and conditions. Under the present act the minister may specify such terms and conditions as he deems to be fair and reasonable, whereas in the bill delivery is to be at current market prices, which in case of dispute may be determined by the exchequer court.
Unlike the present act the bill does not authorize the minister to ascertain fair and reasonable cost and profit and to direct repayment of excess profit.
The bill also calls for the repeal of the Defence Purchases Act. In wartime we had

to set up in great haste to produce munitions and supplies which had never been made before in Canada. There was no fair way of determining in advance what the cost should be, and no time to negotiate. Legislation was enacted to control profits and to provide for the renegotiation of contracts. We then got on with the job, placed contracts and settled the financial outcome later, invoking where necessary the legislative authority. A few of the old contracts are still under examination, or are the subject of pending litigation. There is provision in the bill that in these cases the effect of the present act is preserved.
We consider that in the peacetime conditions of today the control which the government, as a purchaser, exercises over a contractor's profit should be the control which a buyer can exercise in the course of the negotiation and execution of a contract. On this subject I would underline that the proposed bill is designed to meet today's conditions. Emergency conditions would call for new legislation and for an approach to this and other questions in keeping with emergency conditions. As part of our general planning we have draft legislation in readiness for an emergency.

speakeroldname: Mr. George A. Drew (Leader of the Opposition):
subtopic: PROVISION FOR PURCHASE OR ACQUISITION, STORING OF MATERIALS, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this resolution
raises a question which goes far beyond the mere carrying forward of the legislation which has been referred to by the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe). While it is, according to his statement, similar to the legislation known as the Department of Munitions and Supply Act, there are certain variations and certain curtailments which would appear to limit the mandatory authority of the minister in this case. It will not of course be possible to examine these details until the bill is before the house. Nevertheless in this resolution itself, there is sufficient before us now to enable us to consider the principle involved in declaring that it is expedient that such new legislation be introduced as has been described this morning by the minister.
On several occasions during the past year and a half-and I mention a year and a half because that period embraces the three times that the house has met-we have been informed that the procurement agency for the Department of National Defence is the Canadian Commercial Corporation. This does more, therefore, than merely give to the minister in peacetime powers similar to in many respects but less in others than those contained in the wartime Department of Munitions and Supply Act.
One of the questions which immediately arises is this. If the purchasing is to be taken
Defence Supplies
from the Canadian Commercial Corporation, and if that device is not to be employed, why should this function be under the Minister of Trade and Commerce? Why should it not be under the Minister of National Defence himself in peacetime? We are not now talking so much about the individuals concerned as about the principle involved. Except in relation to matters that would normally come under such a broad and embracing department as the Department of Public Works, it has been the general practice for departments to deal with their own requirements. I think that this house should have a great deal more information before it approves in principle the declaration that it is expedient that there be introduced legislation with the wide powers contemplated in this resolution.
I think it is important to indicate the scope and effect of the resolution in peacetime. The resolution reads:
That it is expedient to present a bill, cited as the Defence Supplies Act, to empower the Minister of Trade and Commerce to buy or otherwise acquire and deal with defence supplies; construct or otherwise acquire, projects; acquire, store and otherwise deal with material entering into the manufacture of defence supplies or the development, repair or maintenance of projects; arrange for the performance of commercial and professional services; require priority in delivery or construction and to require persons who have received offers, fair and reasonable in his opinion, for supplies, projects or services, to meet the requirements subject to an appeal to the exchequer court on the question of price; also to empower the minister to buy or otherwise acquire defence supplies and construct or carry out projects required by the Department of National Defence; also to empower the governor in council to appoint assistants to the minister and advisers and advisory boards and to fix their remuneration and expenses; with provision also for the approval by the governor in council of contracts except in emergent cases and where the sum involved does not exceed a certain specified amount.
If the wording of this resolution is to be interpreted in legislation, then without waiting for the bill we are being called upon to declare that it is expedient to turn over to the Minister of Trade and Commerce functions of parliament itself and transactions which will not be subject to the ordinary protection and restraints which over many years have been regarded as important for the protection both of government itself and of the use of the people's money.
There is the provision that the contracts are not to be subject to the requirement of calling for tenders in certain specified cases, four in number. The first of these is when the details are such that the disclosure of them would be regarded as contrary to the public interest. We have seen a great many surprising demonstrations of what is regarded as contrary to the public interest. Hon. members of this house-I am basing this statement on what I have read in

Defence Supplies
Hansard and elsewhere-were obviously reluctant to examine too strictly procedures which, as they stated from time to time, would not be acceptable in peacetime but which in the dreadful emergency of war they were prepared to approve with some concern and with some reservations.
The second specified case is that of this crown corporation which by its authority can deal in activities of this kind; the third is where the contract affects ship repairs and the preparation for the construction of ships; and the fourth, cases in which the government decides that it is contrary to the public interest that there should be any disclosure even of the existence of such a contract because of the danger of conveying to possible enemies knowledge of steps that were being taken; and also certain other cases illustrated by the minister in his remarks.
These are wide exceptions-so wide, in fact, that they would make it possible for the minister to deal in almost any case with projects of this kind without tenders being called for or there being taken those other steps which over long years of parliamentary practice in this country, in Great Britain and in other countries in which there is a similar parliamentary system, have been found to be essential in the public interest. Indeed they have been regarded as so essential that in the case of the Department of Public Works they are explicitly covered by statutory provision.
We are asked to declare that it is expedient that this legislation should replace the Canadian Commercial Corporation as the purchasing agency for the Department of National Defence. With whatever limitations and reservations the bill may contain when it is presented to us, substantially we are being asked to declare as a matter of principle that it is expedient to confer these extremely wide powers in peacetime upon the Minister of Trade and Commerce.
One of the things that must surely impress itself upon the mind of every hon. member, Mr. Speaker, is the difference between the sense of urgency which seems to be implicit in the presentation of this resolution at this time, and the lack of any sense of urgency which was implicit in the position taken by the Minister of National Defence in the discussion of his estimates and in his definite statement that there was nothing new to announce to us in regard to the plans for national defence. The two do not go hand in hand. Either the Minister of National Defence is not disclosing to us all the information in his possession, or there is no immediate need of this resolution and the bill which would follow

it. If there is the need which is indicated by this legislation, then the government should insist that the Minister of National Defence come before us and make a statement as to what the circumstances are that require a revised attitude toward our whole defence problem.
One of the arguments which has not been made, but which could well be made if it has validity, is that the Minister of Trade and Commerce might have referred to the clear statement of the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Pearson) that an historic agreement was made in London a few weeks ago, by virtue of which it had been decided to determine which nation could best produce certain things, best build battleships or aircraft or guns or tanks; that the nation or nations which could best perform that task would be called upon to do the job and that the others would rely upon those nations to supply them.
The Minister of National Defence said something that was not suggested by any member of this house, namely, that the reference to this was an attempt to represent that there was a cleavage between the Minister of National Defence and the Secretary of State for External Affairs. If such a cleavage exists, it is only in the mind of the Minister of National Defence, or to his knowledge; but it certainly is not in the knowledge of any member of this house, because we have no knowledge yet of what the Minister of National Defence wants.

The Minister of National
Defence was critical of any attempt to find out what issue was raised by this new principle so clearly stated by the Secretary of State for External Affairs a week ago today. I should like to refer to the words of the

Minister of National Defence, as reported at page 3457 of Hansard of Friday, June 9. He said, in reference to what I had been asking:
But "Let us know what is needed," he said.
Referring to what I had said, he went on:
And I ask, "Let us know what is needed, where, when, by whom, and with what?"
That is exactly what we were trying to find out. Under this new principle, what is needed, where, when, by whom, and with what? In view of the fact that the Minister of National Defence has told us that there are no changes which he has to announce affecting the general program during the coming year ending March 31 next, surely it is wise for us to ask the Minister of Trade and Commerce, and also perhaps to suggest that the Minister of National Defence ask the Minister of Trade and Commerce, in relation to this legislation:	Let us know what is
needed, where, when, by whom, and with what? We do not know. The Minister of National Defence indicates that he does not know. He explained to us that it was impossible for him to indicate even anything in the future when the bases of decisions have not yet been reached.
If the Minister of Trade and Commerce says to us:	Yes, there is a crisis; these are dangerous days; we must prepare ourselves, I believe most hon. members would agree with that, would agree with measures which would expedite the general activities of this country in relation to every aspect of our defence measures-and obviously the preparation of defence material and the production of defence supplies are almost as vital, if not as vital, as the training of men. Perhaps in some ways it is more fundamental, because, until we have the defence equipment and the defence supplies, much of the training cannot be so carried out on a practical basis as to simulate that measure of realism which prepares men to go into battle if it should become necessary so to do. There certainly must be a measure of urgency indicated by the Minister of Trade and Commerce if the complementary activities are to be regarded as having the urgency which calls for a resolution of this kind. The minister has explained that whereas the act which this is to replace was for the purpose of dealing with an actual state of war, this deals with a period of peace, which nevertheless must be regarded as a period of emergency. He tells us that in this period of emergency circumstances may arise in which mandatory powers will be required. I suggest that if such mandatory powers are required, the simple course to follow is that which was followed in other emergencies-immediately
Defence Supplies
to assemble this parliament so that it may give such mandatory powers as the emergency then apparent demands.
I find it difficult to agree, when the Minister of National Defence tells us that the London decisions presented situations that offer reasons for his projecting changes which a measure such as this would be intended to implement, that the House of Commons has any right in principle to say that it is expedient that these broad powers be conferred upon the Minister of Trade and Commerce.
After all, the house has retained, and the government has made it clear that it has retained, the authority to declare war. Most certainly emergencies far short of war might arise where it would be necessary to deal with such emergencies. It is the hope of each one of us that by recognizing emergencies as they appear, and dealing with them as such, peace may be preserved. I have no doubt the Minister of Trade and Commerce would tell us, and tell us sincerely, that in his opinion the granting of powers of this kind is part of a broad plan to do those things which are essential if we are to play our part in the effort to preserve peace.
In other words, the very name of the act, which abandons the earlier term related to war, does indicate that concept; and I am sure it is a concept of the broad situation in the world today that must meet with the approval of every member of the house. But these wide powers-and they are extremely wide-as explained by the Minister of Trade and Commerce are powers which to a very considerable extent once again would place a large segment of our industrial and other economy beyond the control of parliament, except by way of subsequent examination, and give to the Minister of Trade and Commerce and the government powers which could only reasonably be asked for in a time of war.
The minister has stated that certain mandatory authority will be continued, but he points out that such mandatory powers will be restrained to the extent that the minister does not have power to compel any industry to produce a particular thing. Nevertheless he can establish priorities; and each one of us with any knowledge of what took place during the war years and since knows perfectly well that from the practical standpoint the control of priorities has a mandatory effect upon industries concerned in the exercise of such authority.
The answer may be that these powers are to be exercised only in those cases where industries have voluntarily agreed to produce certain types of equipment or defence

Defence Supplies
supplies. But we all know that from the practical point of view the authority of government over industry today is such that few industries would at any time place themselves in a position where it would be necessary to use compulsion to have them carry out certain tasks. The very fact that these wide powers exist, particularly the power to enter into certain contracts which are not subject to the ordinary provisions of publicity under the four headings explained by the minister, indicates the extent to which a considerable segment of our industrial and other economy would once again come under this very general authority.
In any remarks I am making I am not suggesting that there is no emergency. On the contrary I was taken to task by the Minister of National Defence on Friday for seeking to emphasize the extent of the emergency. I do believe there is one. I believe there is an emergency which has been in no way admitted by the government in the statements made by the Minister of National Defence. The extent of that emergency is indicated by press dispatches such as this one from Washington on May 5:
Defence and state departments of the United States have decided that western powers have at most four years to build up their combined military strength for defence against Russia.
If anything I would think that a generous estimate of the time factor involved. If that is so, then the proper sequence of events to deal with an emergency of that kind is for the Minister of National Defence or the Prime Minister to state to us what the effect of these London agreements really is, and to answer the very question posed by the Minister of National Defence: "Let us know what is needed, where, when, by whom and with what?" Let this parliament know, and then, having let this parliament know, present a resolution of this kind when the members have been informed of the extent of the emergency and of the way in which the emergency is to be met.
Of course most of us read this morning that this is not the business of the opposition. Most of us read this morning the remarkable speech made on Saturday by the Prime Minister, a speech remarkable in its childish arrogance, a speech which said in effect that the role of the opposition was simply to get up and say, "Please, Mr. Speaker, may I make a little suggestion?" and beyond that just to sit and learn. The minister shakes his head, but let me say that I was here in March, 1939, when we had a prolonged discussion on a resolution and bill to set up a defence purchasing board. At the present time we have the Canadian Commercial Corporation, which, so far as the house is aware, has been doing a satisfactory job for the department concerned. Consequently the introduction of a resolution such as this seems to indicate a change in the point of view of the government with regard to the present international situation, a change which, from what I have been able to read, is not warranted.
By chance I was reading, in the British Hansard over the week end, the debate on the defence measures of the United Kingdom. Incidentally I found how different that debate was from the debate which has been proceeding in this house during the past week or so. From time to time the questions asked in this house, and even the answers given, have led me to believe that if I were an agent of the Soviet union all I would do would be to take the Hansard of this House of Commons and send it to Moscow. Indeed it appeared to me that the responsibility in the British house was such that some members were asking for a secret session in order that the kind of information asked for and given in this house during the last week or so could be obtained by the members of the parliament of the United Kingdom.
The resolution before the house differs substantially, and I think gravely, from the resolution preceding the bill of 1939 when there was an emergency foreshadowed. Hon. members will recall that just a few days before the introduction of that measure Hitler had broken his agreement, had overrun Czechoslovakia, was threatening Poland, and

the people of Canada were gravely disturbed. The national defence purchasing board resolution read in part as follows:
That it is expedient to introduce a measure to establish a defence purchasing board with exclusive power, subject to approval of the governor in council, to enter into all contracts for the purchase of munitions, equipment, materials and supplies required by the Department of National Defence in cases where the expenditure exceeds $5,000;-
Then I should like to draw the attention of the house to the following:
-to provide safeguards to assure that such munitions. equipment, materials and supplies shall be purchased at a reasonable cost to the government and without unreasonable profit . . .
The bill subsequently introduced made good the outline given in this resolution. At that time the government was conscious of the fact that public opinion in this country was determined that if we were to engage in an armed conflict and required supplies for our men, those supplies should be provided at least without undue profit to those engaged in their manufacture. While that point of view has not been particularly vocal lately, I believe it still remains substantially the feeling of the Canadian people. Yet under this provision, and after our experience during the war, there is no assurance that this point of view will be recognized in dealing with the appropriations and purchases that may be necessary after this legislation is brought in. As a matter of fact I have before me Hansard for March 10, 1939, when the then minister of national defence, the late Right Hon. Ian Mackenzie, who introduced the resolution and the bill, went into this aspect of the question very thoroughly. At page 1764 he said:
The bill that is to be submitted to this house consequent upon the adoption of the resolution I am now discussing provides that maximum profits upon defence contracts shall not exceed five per cent per annum on working capital actually utilized in the performance of the contract, and this is to be achieved by the simple, clear and definite process of taxing away the excess.
And at page 1767 he went on to say:
The government, if I may speak for them, believe in the principle of equality of sacrifice; that in wartime men should not be required to offer their lives and limbs while those- who provide the weapons of destruction have even the possibility of reaping undue profits.
After the outbreak of war the present Minister of Trade and Commerce, who was then the newly appointed minister of munitions and supply, made the statement that this five per cent limitation had been found unworkable; none the less the government shortly afterward introduced an excess profits tax in an attempt to prevent undue profits from being made during the war. Of course in my opinion-and we may hold and express different opinions in this matter-the minister

did a remarkable job during the war, a job that I believe did him great credit which can never be taken away, no matter what may be said or thought in the future. In doing that job, however, and in cutting through the provisions laid down by parliament, Canadian business did acquire great properties and in that respect made enormous profits out of the war. I am not saying that was done deliberately, but it is a fact. When you examine the capital equipment of industry at the close of the war and for a year or two later, and the manner in which that capital equipment was obtained, you can only conclude that industry in this country did very well out of the war, as indeed was the case in the United States and other countries. But the right hon. gentleman who in 1939 introduced the defence purchasing legislation made it abundantly clear that the government and people of Canada did not expect that when men were called upon to risk their limbs and lives, undue profits would be made by industry. I have before me Hansard for September 12, 1939, where at page 179 the minister said, in reply to a question as to why we were not proceeding under that legislation:
The provision of five per cent was put in the last act after a good deal of consideration as a minimum return for the. service rendered. . . .
I think that word should have been "maximum".

I was saying, as I say now, that the idea behind the defence purchasing board bill of 1939 was one to which I think this house should give quite serious attention. I do not intend to discuss the various clauses in that bill but when the new bill is before the house I think that hon. members might look into that previous bill and might also read the debate which preceded its introduction in 1939.
I was also saying before lunch that I think the people of Canada, though lately not vocal about it, believe that in the preparation for the defence of our country the motive of private gain should be eliminated to the greatest possible extent. In order to achieve that objective I suggest again that we should see to it that industries which are primarily engaged in the manufacture of munitions should be under national ownership and control. I am well aware of the fact that, should war occur, and in preparations for defence, there are many industries which can be converted into munition industries but which are not primarily and fundamentally munition industries. When such industries are engaged on defence contracts or in supplying war materials of every description, in our opinion their profits should be strictly scrutinized and indeed limited. The purchasing board which was set up in 1939 of course had the obligation of limiting profits to 5 per cent on the capital employed in the production of munitions. In looking over the address of the late Right Hon. Ian Mackenzie who

Defence Supplies
at that time was the Minister of National Defence, and from which I quoted to some extent this morning, I find that he said this: The government is determined that in peacetime, where private industry must be utilized, there shall be the strictest possible regulation of profit both in the interest of the taxpayer and in deference to public abhorrence of profits made from products which involve destruction of human lives and misery among nations.
That will be found at page 1767 of Hansard of March 10, 1939. I am sure that that is the opinion of the Canadian people at the present time.
The resolution before us does not foreshadow a bill in any respect resembling the bill that was before the house in 1939. When we look at the amount to be spent in 1939, namely $63 million, in warlike supplies and the amount to be spent now, and when we analyse the $425 million for defence appropriated this year, we realize how much more we are spending on the various types of equipment and on munitions, in the equipment of our forces, than we were spending in 1939. I of course regret, as I have always regretted, that the government at the end of the war saw fit to hand over .to private industry many of the wartime industries that had been set up to make much of the equipment that was made so successfully during the war, and that today we are in many respects without the facilities owned by the people of Canada. To bring the industry again under public control would, and indeed I think should, require that we should repossess ourselves of these particular munition industries.
I do not propose to prolong the discussion at this stage. When the bill is before us I think that the house could go into the matter carefully. I want, however, to express the point of view that we in this party hold, that if we are going to build up defence forces for our country-and we must do so under the conditions that now exist-and if our men are to be properly equipped, I think they must be equipped without any section of the Canadian population, or indeed any population outside Canada, obtaining huge profits from the manufacture of the essential equipment for the defence of our country.

Mr. Speaker, Canada is relatively a small nation-; certainly, it is in so far as her manpower resources are concerned. It seems to me that a deficiency in manpower can be made up by the utilization of our natural resources to the fullest possible measure, thereby providing a reserve which can be made available to ourselves and our allies in an emergency, in case any of those allies of ours should be attacked.

Defence Supplies
Therefore a ready-to-go mobilization plan would ensure that these natural resources would be available the instant an emergency arose. I think that during the past there has been a lack of direction on the part of the government to indicate where industrialists should concentrate their efforts in order that the resources of the country might be made available if and when an emergency arose.
Earlier this year the president of the industrial preparedness association made a nationwide tour. Upon his return he reported that the industrialists in western Canada had complained bitterly that they had not received sufficient information to enable them to do the necessary planning so that, if necessary, they could convert their plants to a point where they would produce those things which would be essential for the supplying of warlike materials to ourselves and our allies. The importance of that planning has been enhanced by the recent decisions made in London within the last month, upon which occasion the means of forestalling the catastrophe of war were examined, and where the new scheme for the collective peace-securing force was initiated, rather than having all the allied powers working on their own and preparing their own limited defence forces.
We have been told also that during the conference great emphasis was placed upon not only the means of preventing war but ways to help in the recovery of Europe. It was urged that there should be collective economic planning so that the various states would be able to direct their resources in the most economical way and in the most effective manner to help in the general recovery.
As I said at the outset of my observations, in many respects Canada is a small country. We cannot spread our endeavours in too many different directions. It is going to be very much a matter of specializing. Therefore one comes back to the question asked last Friday by the leader of this party, "Let us know what is needed." I ask the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe) to give notice to the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Claxton) that the very first question he, the Minister of Trade and Commerce, must ask the Minister of National Defence is this: "Let us know what is needed." To that the Minister of National Defence can give a more effective answer than merely to say, "Let us know what is needed-where, when, by whom and with what."
There is not much use proceeding with this legislation-because it would not be very effective-until the Minister of Trade and Commerce can get those very definite answers. He must be told by the Minister

of National Defence, and perhaps also by the Secretary of State for External Affairs, what is needed; because we cannot just go ahead producing everything and dissipating our efforts in that way. It will have to be specialized planning, and direction will be required. I do not think it is up to the Minister of Trade and Commerce to say what will be produced; he will be told what is required by the Department of National Defence. When the minister replies I would ask him to tell us the system of liaison which will be in operation between the Department of National Defence and the authority now being placed in the hands of the Minister of Trade and Commerce.

Mr. Speaker, I wish to indicate here that I am opposed to the resolution. After listening to the remarks of the various speakers thus far I gather that practically all opposition members are opposed to it, although it may be that we will not oppose it by a formal vote at this stage, when we. have not the details of the bill before us. I do think it is essential that we indicate to the minister that, from the terms of the resolution, our only conclusion can be that the legislation will fulfil our fears in that it will be legislation of the type that should be opposed.
My remarks will be confined chiefly to the fact that at present it appears the legislation contemplated by the resolution is entirely unnecessary. According to the statements made by responsible ministers on those occasions, the Canadian Commercial Corporation, a body which has been discussed on numerous occasions since 1945, was set up to do the very thing we are now asked in this resolution to empower the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe) to do exclusively, or with the assistance of such boards and advisers as he in his discretion may see fit to set up.
Remembering, as one can if he reads the debates of the past, the objections taken to the principles embodied in setting up the Canadian Commercial Corporation, and giving it the wide powers it now has, it surely must be obvious that those of us who held those views must be opposed to duplicating the work of that corporation by setting up further agencies and bodies and giving them the same overlapping and, in some cases, even wider powers than those allotted to the Canadian Commercial Corporation.
I should like to refer to the debates of the last few years so as to remind hon. members what it was intended to do when the Canadian Commercial Corporation was set up, and the powers which in fact were given

to it. On the basis of the statements made by the various ministers who outlined the purposes of that corporation, it appears perfectly clear that with proper direction, it can do all the things this new bill would hand over to the Minister of Trade and Commerce.
In 1947 when the amendment was before us to enlarge the powers of the Canadian Commercial Corporation the then member for Carleton, Mr. Boucher, had this to say as reported at page 4949 of Hansard for July 2, 1947:
The amendment now before the house in effect asks the government to give to that company

That is the Canadian Commercial Corporation.
-the power to produce goods, to manufacture goods, to procure goods and to construct articles in Canada or elsewhere. By this amendment the scope of the activities of the Canadian Commercial Corporation is widened beyond anything comprehended in the original act. The amendment gives this crown company the power to do almost everything possible in the industrial, the economic and even the financial life of our country.
Those were some of the objections which we had at that time to the amendment to the Canadian Commercial Corporation Act, but it goes without saying that the government, having a majority in the house at that time, as they have at the present, saw no merit in our objection to the granting of the powers referred to in that amendment. We find that in the further discussions the powers of the corporation were more specifically defined by the ministers themselves. speechtext: Mr. Chairman, seldom have I heard a debate go so far afield and miss the point of the resolution so completely. This is not legislation to add to the powers of the Minister of Trade and Commerce; it is legislation to take away from his powers. The munitions and supply act is still in force and on the statute books today. I do not know how many hon. members have read that act recently, but if some contractors were to read it now I am sure they would be reluctant to enter into contracts with the government. The munitions and supply act was wartime legislation which gave the minister the widest possible powers; power to renegotiate contracts, power to order a man to accept a contract at prices fixed by the minister, and various other arbitrary powers.

We have not been invoking it recently; nevertheless that is the statute under which the Minister of Trade and Commerce operates today in making defence purchases. The purpose of this legislation is to repeal the munitions and supply act and replace it with legislation limited to powers required in peacetime. These emergency powers we have heard so much about are not new powers; they are a mere fraction of the powers the minister has today. The powers being retained are two in number. One is the power to obtain priority of delivery from a contractor who has signed a contract to supply war materials. We are giving up the right to order a contractor to produce war materials, but if he does contract to produce them and fails to deliver on time, this legislation gives the minister the right to demand priority from that contractor for the delivery of defence projects as against peacetime projects, in the event that the terms of the contract are not being lived up to. The other mandatory power that is retained is the power to requisition materials required to carry out a defence contract. If there is a shortage of lumber and lumber is needed for defence purposes, the Minister of Trade and Commerce can requisition lumber. If there is a shortage of copper and copper is required for defence purposes, the minister can requisition copper. In other words the two powers are first that he may require a government contractor to give priority of delivery under a defence contract he has already signed,
Defence Supplies
and second to requisition material necessary for the carrying out of a government defence contract. I could give you the list of powers that the minister is giving up, but it would take considerable time, and would perhaps shock hon. members to know that powers so arbitrary can still be used in peacetime.

speechtext: We knew that even the minister would not exercise them in peacetime.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR PURCHASE OR ACQUISITION, STORING OF MATERIALS, ETC.
speechtext:
The leader of the opposition said there must be an emergency to justify this legislation. If there were an emergency, we would not be passing this bill. The reason we are passing this bill is that we believe the emergency is past and that we are operating in peacetime. We are operating under the threat of war, but we believe that peacetime is restored to the extent that wartime powers should now be given up and replaced by peacetime powers. The peacetime powers that are being retained in connection with defence purchasing are fewer than those retained by any other country that has defence purchasing legislation. They are far fewer than those under the defence purchasing acts that govern in the United States and fewer than the powers that apply to the Ministry of Supply in the United Kingdom. The point I want to make is that this is a divesting bill rather than a bill adding to the powers of the minister.
The leader of the opposition asked the question:	Why is defence purchasing not
returned to the armed services? I think that the principal reason is that the armed services prefer to have defence purchasing left where it is. They have found that the principle of civilian buying works well, and to the satisfaction of the Department of National Defence. It is rather significant that those countries that resorted to civilian purchasing of defence materials during the war have not returned those powers to the services. In the United Kingdom we had the Department of Supply buying for the army during the war period, and the Department of Aircraft Production buying for the air services.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR PURCHASE OR ACQUISITION, STORING OF MATERIALS, ETC.
speechtext: Does the minister remember when the Department of Supply was set up in England?

subtopic: PROVISION FOR PURCHASE OR ACQUISITION, STORING OF MATERIALS, ETC.
speechtext:
Yes. It was set up just before the outbreak of war, as I recall. Those two United Kingdom departments of government are now combined in the one ministry, the Ministry of Supply; and the purchases for the army and for the air services continue to be made by a civilian department.

Defence Supplies
A good deal has been said about some changed relationship between the armed services and the Canadian Commercial Corporation. I should like to correct a few remarks made in that connection. The Canadian Commercial Corporation was not established to purchase war materials. It was established about 1943 for the purpose of assisting foreign governments to purchase in Canada. It was not until 1946, I think, when the Minister of Munitions and Supply was attempting to wind up his department; and, as this agency was working efficiently, it seemed logical at that time to transfer responsibility for the purchase of military materials from the Minister of Munitions and Supply to the Minister of Trade and Commerce. That transfer was carried out by legislation. The Minister of Trade and Commerce has made use of the Canadian Commercial Corporation to carry out the responsibilities which have been his, just as the Minister of Trade and Commerce in future will use the Canadian Commercial Corporation to exercise the responsibility that is his, namely to make purchases for the armed services. There has been no change in that relationship from the beginning, no change is contemplated, and absolutely no change is suggested in the resolution that is before the committee at this time.
Someone said that if legislation of this kind is needed we should assemble parliament when the emergency arises. Again I say that this is a divesting bill which is being enacted because no emergency confronts this country at the moment. Should an emergency arise, parliament of course will be assembled. A purchasing bill suitable for wartime is in hand and that bill would be placed before parliament at that session. I am sure that parliament would enact that more drastic bill into legislation. But I repeat that what is before parliament now is a bill to govern peacetime purchases.
The leader of the C.C.F. party referred to the Defence Purchases Act, which is also being repealed by the bill that is based on this resolution. The Defence Purchases Act might be described as a noble experiment.
The difficulty came about in attempting to put the legislation into practice. The legislation provided that defence purchases would be made on the basis of 5 per cent on the capital employed in carrying out the contract. If it had been 5 per cent on the cost of the goods, it would have been understandable, and the act might have been effective at least in the vast majority of purchases. The ordinary contract during the war, or rather, the

average of all the contracts placed during the war, varied a profit factor of about 4J per cent. But the act did not say "5 per cent of the cost of the article". It said, "5 per cent return on the capital employed in turning out the article".
How could the amount of capital required be determined? For example, a $100,000 contract might be placed with the Canadian General Electric Company which has a capital of a great many million dollars. How much capital would be required to carry out that $100,000 contract? How could anyone determine that? The government certainly could not determine it, and I doubt if the contractor could determine it. Unless it was agreed that a certain capital would be set aside for the purpose, no one on earth could tell how much the government owed the contractor when that particular contract had been carried out. I think that explains why the Defence Purchases Act, as experience determined, was not an act that could be made operative. It was for that reason that the munitions and supply act was passed shortly after the outbreak of war. It is for that reason that the bill that is based on this resolution repeals the Defence Purchases Act.
I think my statement fairly well covers the points raised in the discussion on the resolution, but I shall be glad to answer any other questions that may be in the minds of hon. members while we are in committee.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR PURCHASE OR ACQUISITION, STORING OF MATERIALS, ETC.
speechtext:
I have listened with a great deal of interest to the discussion and to the minister's explanation. As I understand the matter now, this bill will replace the munitions and 55946-221
Defence Supplies
supply act. In effect the minister says that this new legislation will restrict powers that he had under the munitions and supply act. We will have to take the minister's word for that. On reading the resolution upon which the bill is to be based, I think the powers are unlimited.
As many hon. members have indicated, this is peacetime legislation. We are not living in a peaceful world. I assume that the powers are delegated here, having in mind that in the event of an emergency the machinery that is ready can be put into operation to take care of the emergency. It might mean that the powers are emergency powers. Personally I am not objecting to that. My reason for rising was to say I trust that both in peacetime and in the event of an emergency these powers will be exercised a little more realistically with regard to the placing of our defence projects than they were during the last war. During the last war there was a' complete concentration of our munitions industries, and generally our war industries in the two central provinces. They were pretty well bundled together, to the extent that in Ontario a power shortage was created as an aftermath of the war.
When the war ended, of course, all the industries were handed over to someone for very little money. The matter of decentralization of industry in the event of another emergency is a live issue in the United States today, and it should be a live issue in Canada.
The minister has been working through the Canadian Commercial Corporation, and he says that he intends to continue to do so. The machinery is not changing at all. All they are doing is changing the name of the body that is to do the purchasing under the same minister. Apparently that organization has been functioning for some time. I think the same trend that has been apparent over the years, namely, the concentrating of everything in the two central provinces, is. being followed. This matter has been the subject of inquiry and investigation. The Dawson commission report on this very question is a strong indictment of this thing, with particular reference to the denuding of the maritimes and western Canada. The Agures are there. I am not going to repeat them. Anyone can look them up.
What I am disappointed in is this. Recently the minister put out a report on private and public investment in Canada, outlook for 1950. On page 4 of the introduction to the report he sets out that there is a forecast of public and private investment amounting to $3.6 billion for 1950. In looking over the report I And that so far as Prince Edward Island, Nova Scotia and New Brunswick are concerned, their share, the total maritime share of that potential investment, is around 6.67 per cent-practically nothing.

Defence Supplies
In the light of international complications today we are wise in providing legislation that is workable in peacetime and could be used in an event of an emergency. I think the efforts of the department of munitions and supply in the concentration of industry in one spot that could be knocked out with a few bombs was unrealistic in the last war. I think too it was bad for the whole economy of the country. The terrific public investment made during the war in plant and industry across the country was lost in the aftermath of the war; it was practically given away to private industry. I am not objecting to this machinery. I am in hopes that, with the experience of the past and with the machinery that is being set up having to do with the regulation of public investment, in the event of an emergency some regard will be had to keeping the major industries decentralized so far as that may be possible, not only because of power and other factors, but because I think in the event of war you are going to be hit quickly from the air with something pretty powerful. If you have too much concentration in one spot it will be easy to knock it out overnight. The forecast of public and private investment for 1950 certainly does not indicate anything along these lines, because the same old concentration is taking place in the same two provinces.
I should like to endorse what the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar had to say in emphasizing government ownership. You can call it nationalization, socialization, or whatever you like; I believe that the munitions industry, which will be created largely by government funds, should be in large measure under government control. The government should have control over the munitions industry in the event of wars and prior to war, because I believe there will always be wars as long as there is money to be made out of them.
I am not going to emphasize that matter now. We have discussed it time and time again. I have always been convinced that nobody should make any profit out of war. We are all in it together. You requisition the lives of the young people and send them to fight for the institutions of the country. Why should the fellow who stays at home make a lot of money? When the war is over, the blood, sweat and tears employed in it should be the payment in full. There should not be interest charges. But that is not the issue at this time. I wish to leave that thought with the minister when he proceeds to his discussions with those who are going to set up in this country plants and industry which may be used for defence purposes. That should be decentralized and scattered across the country to the greatest possible extent.
[Mr. Gillis.l
When we build plant and equipment for an emergency I think we should keep in mind what can be done with that plant and equipment after a war, so that we might level off the economy of the country. I am not opposed to the resolution. I believe that under circumstances such as exist today we must be ready for emergencies. It is not good enough to begin doing that after something hits us. The machinery should be ready now. I am accepting the minister's statement that this is merely a process of transferring the operations under the Department of Munitions and Supply Act to the Canadian Commercial Corporation, which seems to be doing a pretty good job.
I am not objecting to that; but I do object to the concentration of industry in the two central provinces. I say that is bad planning for defence, and I have risen at this time to focus the attention of the minister on that point.

Ian Mackenzie, then minister of national defence, who introduced the bill, went out of his way to make it clear that that was the government's position. Defence Supplies

Far from doing that, the best protection the government can have is an experienced purchasing staff, a staff that knows the capacity of the country and its capacity for turning out anything the government wishes to buy, as well as the cost of operation of any industry. subtopic: PROVISION FOR UNIFORM SYSTEM OF PUBLISHING REGULATIONS AND LAYING THEM BEFORE PARLIAMENT

speechtext: The house resumed, from Wednesday, May 31, consideration of the motion of Mr. St. Laurent for the second reading of Bill No. 89, to provide for the publication of statutory regulations.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR UNIFORM SYSTEM OF PUBLISHING REGULATIONS AND LAYING THEM BEFORE PARLIAMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on May 31, when the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) moved the second reading of this bill, he explained the bill. I think it is only proper to say that we in this party are in agreement with the intentions of the bill as indicated by the Prime Minister. We feel that a real attempt has been made to place statutory orders, regulations, orders in council and so on, on a footing where it will be more feasible than it has been in the past for members and others interested to ascertain what is in the orders and regulations and how they are affected by them. However, there are one or two reservations which we have with respect to the bill and which I should like to indicate, and there are certain questions we would like the Prime Minister to answer when we are in the committee stage.
Although we now have a statute which as I read it provides for the consolidation of all effective orders and regulations up to the present time, and of which the Prime Minister tabled the first volume in the house recently, the bill goes on to provide for a system of consolidation of subsequent orders in council and regulations but the method by which that publication and consolidation is to be carried on is in turn to be left to order in council. We would have preferred if it had been possible to have had some specific provision in the bill as to how this was to be done and the basis upon which it was to be carried out. As the situation is at present, under section 9 there is provision for the future publication and consolidation, but that is left to the governor in council by regulation.
I do not refer to the fact that there are statutory requirements for publication in the Canada Gazette, for the laying on the table of parliament within certain statutory periods of regulations and orders in council, except such as may be excepted by order in council, but rather to such regulations governing future consolidations along the lines of the volume already tabled and which are to be left to order in council. I think it would have been desirable if at least an outline of that system could have been incorporated in the bill itself.
It is appreciated that this task of providing adequate publicity for orders in council and regulation and ensuring that all those who are affected shall have a chance to know what they are before they become law is a difficult one, and the whole problem of delegated legislation under present-day conditions of carrying on government is bound to be a difficult one. Therefore I think the Prime Minister and the house will appreciate the import of my remarks, that it would be

desirable if we could have a statutory definition of how these things are to be published.
One will recall that in the past orders in council and regulations did not have the effect of law until they had been passed by the house in the form of a bill, not simply being tabled. Orders in council that had been laid upon the table were given second reading and it was only after they had been formally approved by the House of Commons that they had the force of law.
My authority for this statement is to be found at page 2382 of Hansard of May 22, 1918, where the following is to be found under the heading "Concurrence in orders in council":

that the orders in council laid on the table of the house on the 2nd April, 1918, be concurred in. He said: The orders in council which have been issued and laid on the table form a long list of two pages. They are formal to a certain extent, but the law requires that these orders in council when passed shall be laid on the table of the house within a certain time.
That is the situation at the present time. Orders in council have to be laid on the table of the house generally fifteen days after they are passed, or if parliament be not then sitting, within fifteen days of the commencement of the next session. Then Sir George Foster continued:
I think they are not law until they are so laid on the table of the house, and thereafter if approved by the house.
Sir Wilfrid Laurier replied:
These orders in council, as I understand the law, have to be submitted to the house and ratified by the house.
