speechtext:
As a rule these orders in
council are considered in committee of the whole because it is more convenient to discuss them in committee than with Mr. Speaker in the chair. I have looked at the orders in council referred to in the motion and I see nothing of any importance in them, so that possibly we can approve of them without going into committee, if my hon. friend will call attention to any particular one of them which may be of importance. As I am advised at present, and from a cursory glance at them, I see nothing objectionable. They appear to be in most respects merely technical orders in council.
I refer to that to show that the discussions we have had on the practice of order in
Regulations Act
council government and the dangers inherent therein are by no means to be passed over lightly because so seriously was it regarded at the end of the first world war that these orders in council and regulations, which were laid on the table of the house in pursuance of statutory requirements, did not in fact become law until concurrence of the house had been formally moved and granted. I am not going to go so far as to move an amendment to the bill at this time to incorporate in it any such provision, but I think it gives force to the suggestion that it would have been desirable if the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent), while going as far as he has, after a great deal of careful study and consideration, to provide that orders in council and regulations will be fully known and understood so that those affected may know what laws they have to operate under, had gone a little further and provided in the bill he has introduced actual statutory provisions governing their publication and consolidation instead of leaving that in turn to be made the subject of an order in council. With these observations, however, I say that we concur in the bill and approve its objectives. We would like more information as to the classes or types of orders in council which it is intended to exempt by regulation from the provisions of this statute with regard to consolidation and publication. We would also like more information as to the method which it is proposed to follow in the future to provide for that consolidation and publication.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR UNIFORM SYSTEM OF PUBLISHING REGULATIONS AND LAYING THEM BEFORE PARLIAMENT

Mr. Speaker, I will take only a moment or two because generally speaking this bill strikes us as a piece of good legislation. Indeed anything that makes it more clear to parliament and to the general public just what the laws of the land are is all to the good. We have got to the situation where regulations passed under statutes are far more numerous than the statutes themselves, and in the very nature of things they, are a part of the law of the land. The two or three reservations mentioned by the hon. member for Kamloops (Mr. Fulton) have been in my mind as well. I shall not take time to spell them out. He used almost the exact language that I had intended to use when he said he hoped that the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) would give us a little clearer statement as to the classes of regulations which the government has in mind with reference to the clause providing for exemption from the requirement that all regulations be tabled and published.
In fact I noted when the Prime Minister made his speech on second reading of the bill he said that the publishing and tabling of

Regulations Act
all regulations would now be made compulsory, and I took it at the time that was an unequivocal statement. There is in the bill, however, the exemption clause, which we would like to have explained fully at some stage of the debate today. The other comment I should like to make is that I -trust the bill will be passed in time for its effect upon a great host of statutes to reach the commission revising the statutes of Canada. I note that a good many statutes will have sections repealed or a few words struck out of a section, and I think it would be desirable when the Revised Statutes of Canada appear that those changes should be incorporated therein.
The Prime Minister might also say a word when he replies, or when we get into committee, with respect to the tabling of reports. When the legislation was first forecast, as a matter of fact by comments made by the Prime Minister during the last session, I thought it was going to cover both regulations passed under statutes and reports of departments that are laid on the table of the house each session. The same lack of uniformity applies in connection with those reports as in the case of regulations. The period of time within which a departmental report must be laid upon the table varies from ten days in some cases to fifteen in others, and longer periods in others. As a matter of fact I believe there are some departments which are not required by statute to place their reports on the table of the house, although I believe in most cases they do. It would seem to me that it is desirable that there should be uniformity in that regard as well. I would appreciate it if at some stage of the discussion the Prime Minister would indicate whether that matter has been given consideration, and with what result. I need not take longer because, as I said at the beginning of my remarks, generally speaking we think this is a piece of good legislation.

speechtext:
I should like to refer to a matter mentioned in the speech of the Prime Minister in which there appears to be some contradiction which might be cleared up. At page 3039 of Hansard the right hon. gentleman said:
This procedure was established by order in council P.C. 4876 on the 26th of November, 1946, under authority conferred by section 30 of the Public Printing and Stationery Act.
At that point he was referring to the procedure of publication in the Canada Gazette. In the next paragraph the Prime Minister referred to the consolidation of such statutory orders and regulations in effect on December 1, 1949, as having been prepared and in the hands of the king's printer; that is the volume now before us. He then went on to say:
The order in council to which I have just referred is known as "The statutory orders and regulations order, 1947."
In trying to follow the discussion I find myself at a loss because I am not sure whether there were two different orders in council, the one of November 26, 1946, and another fti 1947, which I could not find, or whether the reference to the statutory orders and regulations order, 1947, should have read "1946".

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
subtopic: PROVISION FOR UNIFORM SYSTEM OF PUBLISHING REGULATIONS AND LAYING THEM BEFORE PARLIAMENT
speechtext:
No, I think 1947 is correct. It was called the statutory orders and regulations order, 1947, because it was intended to operate as from January 1, 1947, and at that time it was intended to separate the ordinary notices in the official gazette from the statutory orders and regulations which were published in a different form.
With respect to this definition, I want to state again that we found it would not be possible or prudent to make statutory exemptions with respect to the application of this statute. We wanted it to include everything, to make it necessary for us to call attention to anything that was not going to be governed by it. So we said we would make it as sweeping as possible so it would apply to every kind of order that has legislative effect, made
Regulations Act
under authority given by parliament; and if we wanted to take anything out of that general, sweeping declaration we would have to call attention to what we were taking out so if there should be any controversy as to whether it should be in or out the matter would be brought to the attention of hon. members and the public. This would apply to a great many things if we did not make exceptions. It would apply, for instance, to all the orders given from time to time from the control towers at our airfields. Of course no one would want those published in permanent form, for they operate once and are spent. We have quite a variety of things of that character which are spent immediately, and which will be excepted from the application of this act.
This legislation will apply not only to the regulations made by the government, either the governor in council, treasury board, or boards or commissions set up by parliament. It will apply to regulations made by railway companies, for instance, if those regulations, by virtue of federal legislation, have the sanction of a penalty in the form of a fine or imprisonment. Railways make bylaws for the proper conduct of their passengers. If those bylaws are sanctioned, by virtue of a federal statute, by a penalty in the form of a fine or imprisonment for violation, they will have to be registered and published. We thought it desirable to have something comprehensive, that could be relied upon as containing the complete picture of the things having the force of this parliament behind them, and that we would have to specifically indicate everything that was not going to be included in the general, sweeping assertion.

Subsection 3 of this section
6 provides:
No regulation Is invalid by reason only that it was not published in the Canada Gazette . . .

Then it goes on to provide that no person shall be convicted of an offence unless it was proved that the regulation was exempted from publication, and that reasonable steps had been taken to bring it to the notice of the person affected. I would not ask the Prime Minister to tell us or to attempt to tell us here what would be accepted as evidence of "reasonable" in a court of law. That is not the implication of my question. I would ask him, however, if he would tell us what steps are considered reasonable by the government and what steps are in fact taken to bring to the attention of the persons affected such regulations as are not published?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
subtopic: PROVISION FOR UNIFORM SYSTEM OF PUBLISHING REGULATIONS AND LAYING THEM BEFORE PARLIAMENT
speechtext:
Because of the sweeping
terms of the definition "regulations", it will include all sorts of orders; and it may be that, for instance, some regulation of a railway company had not been published and the penalty for infringement sanctioned by a section of the Railway Act is fine or imprisonment. If it had not been published, and there had not been, to the satisfaction of the court, the publicity given to it that made the offender a voluntary offender, the court would not convict.
In these matters I think it is better not to attempt to bind the courts down too tightly. I think this statute will show that it was not the intention of parliament that everything be published, and that considerable discretion should be left to the court, if one was prosecuted under an order that was not published, in determining whether or not the offender should be looked upon as having done something that he knew was wrong. I think it is preferable to leave that.
Then the circumstances may vary. There might be an occasion when there would be a question about the regularity of registration and publication. The hon. member will notice that we require the order to be sent to the clerk of the privy council to be recorded, and then the publication is required to be made within a certain time after that is done. A question might arise, although it had been published in the official gazette, as to whether it was done within the proper time after the recording in the privy council office. I think it is better to leave it to the courts to apply in a manner that will make it workable rather than to be too specific about it. If something had been published simultaneously with the recording or if it had been sent to the official gazette at the same time at it was sent to the privy council, and if as a matter of fact it were established that the clerk of the privy council had not recorded it until the day after it was published in the Gazette, the question might
Regulations Act
arise whether that was compliance with the statute. I think those matters should be left for the common-sense determination of those presiding over the courts.

speechtext:
I appreciate the principle that the Prime Minister has suggested. What limited experience I have had does suggest that courts, on the other hand, have great difficulty in interpreting the word "reasonable" in a statute such as this. I am thinking particularly of an instance where a regulation is in the exempted class, and it is not necessary to publish in the Gazette. It will be difficult to say what are the reasonable steps which should have been taken to bring it to the attention of the person affected. I am wondering whether the Prime Minister would consider putting the onus more upon the authority publishing the regulation to bring it to the attention of the person affected. If the words "all necessary steps" were substituted here for the words "reasonable steps" so that it would read:
Unless
(b) it is proved that at the date of the alleged contravention all necessary steps had been taken-
-and so on, that would bring the matter to the attention of the person affected. I think these words would clearly establish not only the onus of proving that it had been brought to his attention but the necessity of taking the steps necessary to bring it to his attention would be on the body making the order or the regulation.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
subtopic: PROVISION FOR UNIFORM SYSTEM OF PUBLISHING REGULATIONS AND LAYING THEM BEFORE PARLIAMENT
speechtext: Let me suggest this case. An order goes out from a control tower in an airfield to a plane that is coming in, and the apparatus in that plane is not in a position to receive the message; and because of the neglect of the pilot, or of the owner of the plane, he is not in a position to receive the message. Well, the sending of the message would not be all the necessary steps to bring it to his attention. What would have been necessary to bring it to his attention would have been an inspection of the plane to make sure that there was a private receiving apparatus in his plane. Well, that would not be reasonable. Today if one attempts to use public airfields one is supposed to be in a position to receive the directions that come from the control towers. I think that no court would find it difficult to say that it would not be an excuse for him to say: "Well, my receiving set was out of order and that is why I did not comply with the order I got from the control tower." These orders from the control towers will certainly be in the exempted class.

No; the exempting order will be published, and it may be merely a temporary order. For instance, at Chalk River there may be an order made that a certain area for a certain number of weeks would be out of bounds. It might be felt that for security reasons it was inadvisable to call the attention of the general public to that. No one could be prosecuted under that unless it had been brought to his attention. But if it were at Chalk River, the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre and I as member for Quebec East would not be interested at all. It would have to be shown that there had been indications in the immediate locality bringing that order to the attention of those who might be affected by it.
We had quite a discussion over the necessity of even publishing the order made exempting such things because of their security implications; but the decision was that we wanted to give as complete information as possible, and that we would have to take the risk. If there was something of a legislative character that was not going to be published we would have to take the risk of describing it as an excepting order, and we would have to make the excepting order public so that all members of parliament could question the propriety of our doing it. We wanted in no way to call attention to everything that was not going to come under the general provisions of the statute.

I should like to ask the minister a question with regard to little cherry disease. This is a matter of great interest to cherry growers in the interior of British Columbia. The report which I have here on little cherry disease indicates that it is caused by a virus and that it continues to spread in the Kootenay and Arrow lake districts, as revealed by surveys conducted by dominion and provincial officials. The insertion of buds from diseased cherry trees into peach, prune, apricot, choke cherry and wild cherry and of buds of peach, prune and choke cherry growing near diseased cherry trees into healthy trees, and the artificial pollination of healthy cherry trees with pollen from diseased trees all failed to produce any clear-cut symptom the following year, as it would be expected if the little cherry disease had been transmitted. A tree-to-tree survey was conducted in the Okanagan valley by provincial officials, with assistance from the staff of the Summerland laboratory of plant pathology, and which covered all the southern part and up to the end, including Kelowna. No tree with definite symptoms of little cherry disease was found. One tree in the Oliver district was removed on suspicion.

Mr. Chairman, this department administers a great industry in Canada, and I hope hon. members will not question the additions to staff that are so necessary. Throughout the years there have been shortages in staff in many of the provinces, and I am quite sure farmers of this country are pleased to see work being done that has been neglected for some years.
So far as travelling expenses are concerned, it is my opinion that the men working in this department cannot do a good job unless they travel. It has been my experience that officials of the Department of Agriculture travel as cheaply as those of any department of government. I have found them on many occasions seeking to get accommodation by getting rides, and have even found them trying to cut down expenses to the extent of borrowing my own broncho and buggy.
I understand the minister's department is conducting investigations in connection with forest insect tests in conjunction with the forest service of the Department of Resources and Development. Some investigation is being carried on in the interior of British Columbia. How many men are engaged in that work at the present time, and what work is contemplated during the coming season in that area?

The hon. member is correct when he says that the Department of Agriculture does research work in this connection. We conduct research into the matter of providing parasites to fight other insects. We breed armies of them and arrange to have them turned loose so that they may put up a battle against the worms which damage the crops and the forests. That kind of work is done in our laboratories, and these insects, are put out. The best illustration which comes to my mind, offhand, was the cutworm, infestation of my own farm on one occasion. These little insects we have bred and put out were there in large numbers. After a rain, when the cutworms had to come above the ground to get air, these insects were darting around the place, stinging each worm, and gradually wiped them out.
Then, we do breed parasites that prey upon insects and worms which damage crops and forests in general. That is our end of:

the work; but the work of actually fighting the difficulties that arise in the forests is not under this department.

The other day I asked a question about the worm or caterpillar which attacks the oak, basswood, maple, elm and other trees. I believe at the present time they are found in great numbers in Muskoka, and have gone up to Haliburton. They travel by the million, and when they cross a road it is absolutely black with them. They will bleed a tree in half an hour.
A kind of yellowish black.
They are green in colour, and range from one to two inches in length. What is the government doing about this pest?

There are different ways of dealing with them. 1 do not know about the particular movement of army worms to which the hon. member has referred, but we have worms of that kind in the west, and I believe they are found in all parts of Canada at different times. One method of dealing with them is to put tarpaper around the bottom of the tree, and then put grease on it. But one should be properly informed before he begins to do that. A whole row of trees on my own place were killed by a man who stopped reading where the instruction said to put on the grease; he did not note that it had also said to put tarpaper on the tree first. This man put the grease around the bottom of the trees and killed them more effectively than the worms would have done. So it is necessary to inform oneself properly before beginning to fight these pests.
However, there are successful methods of fighting them, depending of course upon the nature of the worm. The method I have described is one that is followed in fighting the army worm-that is, to put grease on paper around the bottom of a tree, so that they will not go up the tree. However we have found in the west that, so far as that particular grub is concerned, they do not actually kill the trees. They take the leaves off the tree and there is a dropping of sap to the extent that you almost need an umbrella when walking underneath. But the leaves come on again and the trees continue to live. For example, some three or four years ago the leaves came off the apple trees down around Trenton three times in the season for different reasons, one being frost, but eventually most of the trees lived. The battle has to be continued against them, but one has to be careful whether he sprays or what he does in order to deal with them in the right manner and at the right time. I think those who
Supply-Agriculture
are familiar with the necessity of fighting pests of that kind know the method to use in connection with their own operations.

I would like the minister to come up to our part of the country where we have some million trees and try to put tarpaper around them. The oak trees are suffering especially. The leaves came off some of them last year and today some of those trees are dead while others are only half alive, the tops being gone. With the leaves going this year again on the same trees I am afraid they will die. I wonder if some other method could be used than the tarpaper and grease. We have tried that but you can handle only a few trees with that method. If you use D.D.T. from the air you kill the birds and then you are worse off than before.
Has the minister's department discovered why the apples from Sim-coe county are so far superior in all respects to those from British Columbia? *

Have any effective means been discovered to deal with the aphides that are affecting grain at the present time? I understand that this pest is now to be found in Manitoba and if it is not treated successfully, sooner or later it will reach the other provinces.

The campaign being carried on against the green aphides is the same as that carried on against the grasshoppers. We undertake to map the different areas that may be infested and the provincial government does the actual work to combat the insect.

I think it would be most useful if the minister could give us a little more information about this pest. We had a considerable infestation in our part of the country last year. A rather expensive poison was brought in from the United States but it was so deadly people were frightened to use it because there were reports of loss of life in the United States from its use. Then we are told that where crops are sprayed in an effort to kill weeds apparently there are also killed those parasites that would take care of these aphides. In my neighbourhood crops that were sprayed for this purpose were those that suffered most severely from this infestation.

I am instructed by the officials that so far as they know there is no relationship between spraying the crop and the infestation; it is a matter of weather conditions rather than actual spraying. The green aphid or green bug appeared suddenly in enormous numbers in southern Manitoba and southeastern Saskatchewan and inflicted extensive damage. They were reported from widely scattered points in southern British Columbia. Normally this insect is

Supply-Agriculture
a severe pest in the southern United States and occasionally appears in numbers in the Dakotas, Minnesota and Wisconsin but is rarely found in Canada. It is not known whether this insect can successful pass the winter in Canada but it is generally supposed that the Canadian infestations are a direct migration from further south. The green bug appeared so suddenly last year and in such enormous numbers that it was thought quite unlikely that they had developed locally. Pyrethrum sprays gave a good deal of control when used in a control campaign. 1 am referring to the 1949 report.

I understand that the two per cent wettable spray which is not allowed into Canada is not nearly as dangerous as the fifteen per cent powder spray that is available. Has the minister any information on that?
We would have to know the content of the powder or the liquid before we could give definite information.

This is a particular chemical that is used to kill aphides and it is the only one that can be bought in large quantities. There is considerable danger in mixing this dry powder while there is not nearly the danger in using the two per cent wettable or fluid mixture. I suggest that the department get in touch with the customs and excise branch to see if the less dangerous material cannot be allowed to enter the country.

Could the minister have someone from his department go into the northern parts of Victoria and Haliburton counties to see if anything can be done about the army worm that is destroying great stretches of forest in those areas?
There are men up there on that work at the present time.

I hope I will see the hon. member when I am in that area.

The constituency of Medicine Hat happens to be one that does not have an experimental farm with the exception of the dominion range station which has been of wonderful value not only to the ranchers of that area but to many others. The citizens of Medicine Hat have one complaint concerning it, that it is too far away from the city. It is a distance of about eighty or eighty-five miles from Medicine Hat to the range station. The Manyberries range station has been specializing in grass and investigating the number of cattle that a quarter section can support. In addition they have small fruits and trees which they have shown can be produced on similar irrigation projects where there is a supply of water.
No doubt the minister knows the range station quite well. A coulee has been dammed off where they store the water from the spring run-off, and they utilize it during the summer. The majority of the citizens of Medicine Hat never see the range station, and in view of the fact that we expect great irrigation developments in that area within the next three or four years I believe it would be to the advantage of everyone there if the Department of Agriculture should see fit to open a new experimental station close to Medicine Hat. There is a small irrigation project at Ross creek, and part of that land

could be easily utilized to show what can be done by irrigation. I should like to ask the minister if any consideration has been given to having an experimental farm established close to the city of Medicine Hat so that the people of that area can really see what can be done when you provide some water for the land.

The experimental farms we have across Canada are of many different kinds. They are placed in different areas to do the work required in those areas. The region south of Medicine Hat has been a ranching area, and while it is quite true that the station at Manyberries is located beside a pool of water created by damming a creek, nevertheless we have 30,000 acres of land in that region with which we are experimenting. I think it is by far the largest experimental operation in Canada. We have 30,000 acres of land leased from the provincial government, and the primary purpose of the experiment is to find out whether or not grasses which can be sown in that area will maintain more cattle per acre than the natural grass, or what the relationship is between the grasses. My understanding is they have found it requires about 30 acres of natural prairie to maintain an animal. That will indicate to people in eastern Canada who maintain thirty or forty on a hundred acres of land that ranching is an undertaking which requires a considerable amount of land. That is the experimental work necessary in that section and the work which is done there. Very close checks are kept. I have gone over a considerable part of the area, examined the markings they have and the manner in which they test the number of cattle that can be run on the different acreages. The work is very successfully carried on, and I think it is most helpful to people living in that section.
As to the other areas, I think nearly all of the irrigation districts have special experimental stations. As the hon. member for Medicine Hat knows, the operation at Brooks is a provincial one and there is experimental work carried on there. We have other experimental stations in connection with other operations in Alberta, and I think it is generally acknowledged that they are as well supplied with that kind of station as any of the provinces of Canada.

I realize that the Manyberries
range station has done wonderful work so far as grazing land is concerned. We have a provincial station at Brooks, but as the minister knows it is mostly concerned with horticulture. We have substations throughout the area where test plots are operated by the elevator companies. I believe it is the wheat pool and the Searle Grain Company that have
Supply-Agriculture
small plots throughout the district growing certain kinds of grain, but they are insufficient to give the people a real idea of what can be grown there. I see no reason why we should not have an experimental station closer to Medicine Hat where the people could see what can be done with irrigation. There are many areas similar to the Manyberries range station where dams can be built, the spring run-offs held back and many grasses, grains and fruits grown. I think that would be most beneficial to Medicine Hat especially in view of future irrigation developments.
I appreciate the wonderful work that has been carried on at the Manyberries range station. As the minister said, it requires about 30 acres of land per head of cattle per year. Many eastern members might want to dispute that but it must also be remembered that the provincial government lease their lands on the basis of three head per quarter section, 160 acres. Wonderful results have been achieved at the Manyberries range station, but we would like to see a station established closer to Medicine Hat, perhaps on the Ross creek irrigation project, or some place within easy driving distance of the city. Then the people could see what can be done. I think it is a good idea and a timely one.

I should like to ask the minister how many employees there are currently at the Lacombe experimental farm, and also the amount of damage incurred during the storm from which they suffered last autumn. I understand it was quite considerable.

Last year there were
drought, hail and frost.
The particular storm I was referring to was a windstorm which blew down many of the trees.

I have no particular report on a windstorm. They tell me there was hail damage, which probably went along with the wind, and that there was also damage at that farm last year from drought and frost. I will get the number employed at the farm.
While you are looking that up, if you cannot give me a break-down on the storm damage perhaps you can tell me the cost of upkeep for that station last year.
The cost of the Lacombe farm last year was $147,395. This year it will be $203,048, an increase of $55,653. That increase is largely accounted for by a building item.

May I ask the minister if his department has given any consideration to establishing an experimental farm at Medicine Hat.

Supply-Agriculture

The best experimental plot I have even seen in western Canada is only about a mile away from Medicine Hat. It is not operated by the government, or was not when I was familiar with it. I refer to the area just west of the town, where they have pump irrigation. The first time I went to Medicine Hat to investigate anything they took me there to show me the good job that had been done by the two men who were working as partners handling and feeding cattle. They grew corn, sunflowers and everything that can be grown, by means of irrigation; and they fed cattle very successfully. As far as the government is concerned, as my hon. friend knows we are endeavouring to develop the Vauxhall area just as soon as we can get title to the land, so we hope it will not be too long before we will have an experimental station there. That is within easy distance of Medicine Hat; it does not take very long to get out there, and that is certainly under consideration. I cannot say any other area is under consideration at the moment.

Even the Vauxhall area is sixty or seventy miles north of Medicine Hat, and we would like a station closer than that. The farm to which the minister refers, where they grow corn and feed cattle, is but one of a number of such farms all along the river, both east and west of Medicine Hat. These small irrigation projects, where they pump the water from the river, have been very successful, but the people of Medicine Hat want a farm with nice trees, where they can really spend an enjoyable day. There is plenty of land within a few miles of the city that could be utilized for this purpose, and that is their request at the present time.
Is there any revenue from the central experimental farm at Ottawa?
The total revenue is about $400,000.

I wonder if the minister would care to comment on the work being done at the experimental farms of Canada in connection with artificial insemination. I have had the opportunity of discussing this matter with the minister, and I know he has carried on some investigations during his visit to Europe. This is something we must face sooner or later, and I believe it is a step in the right direction. If you want to increase your milk production this is the best way to do it. In three years you could have practically the same amount of milk from about seventy-five per cent of the cows now required. I believe something has been done in that connection at the Kemptville farm,

and this spring I had the opportunity of visiting one of the stations operated by the Scottish milk board, where they have had wonderful success.
There is another feature to it. Every year in Canada at least half a dozen farmers are killed by bulls. Artificial insemination would do away with that danger on the farm. It is also cheaper. Some bulls in Britain cost ten thousand guineas today; but by this method, instead of getting just an ordinary heifer that will give maybe 800 gallons of milk, a farmer can get a cow that will give perhaps 1,200 gallons of milk. This means that with fewer but better animals the milk production can be increased. I do not know how it would work with beef cattle, but as far as the dairy breeds are concerned it has been a great success. I would be glad if the minister would comment on this matter for my own personal information, if not for the benefit of the rest of the committee. It seems to me that it would be a wonderful thing for farmers who have only from eight to twenty cows, and no bulls, to be able to get heifer calves that would be really worth something in the market.

Of course the proper item under which this should be discussed is production services, but for the moment I might just say that in the Fraser river valley we did assist by supplying bulls for this purpose, and we have also assisted in the same way at Truro, Nova Scotia. That is about as far as we can get from Manitoba in both directions. Most of that kind of work is done by the provinces. In Ontario, for example, experimental work is being carried on at Kemptville. I have seen the activities there, and I quite agree that very helpful work can be done. I also understand that some prominent breeders in Ontario carry on this work themselves, no doubt with some assistance from the provincial government. At Dryden farm, for example, they do a good deal of that kind of breeding, and I think it is becoming quite a common thing elsewhere. However, we are not promoting it beyond providing some bulls in certain areas for these purposes.

I wonder if this would be the proper item under which I might return to a question I asked the minister some little time ago with respect to the apparent duplication of scientific experts as between the Department of Trade and Commerce and the Department of Agriculture. At that time the minister made a very interesting speech, in the first part of which he more or less gave me an answer, and in the latter part of which he ranged all over the place in a very delightful manner. I realized that I had served a very useful purpose by giving the

minister an opportunity to make that speech which no doubt had been in his mind, but now I want to come back to my question. He partly answered it by pointing out that there was an apparent duplication in the selling agencies but that it was only apparent, because the Department of Trade and Commerce had the foreign field in which to operate while the Department of Agriculture had the domestic field. That was his answer as I recall it. At that time I think the minister said nothing with regard to the apparent duplication of scientific officers, of whom there are quite a number. If this is the proper place to ask this question, perhaps the minister would indicate to us how many scientific officers there are; how many officers there are in the Department of Trade and Commerce dealing with scientific agricultural subjects and how many there are, roughly, in the Department of Agriculture, and satisfy us that there is in fact no duplication, if that is a fact.

I do not know of any scientific agriculturists in the Department of Trade and Commerce. My officials tell me that that is true, that there are not any as far as they know. There are some what might be called scientific operators in the Department of Resources and Development which has to do with fighting pests in the forests and that sort of thing. Their work does not overlap with ours but there is co-operation between the two departments in operating there. So far as I know, however, there are no scientific specialists in the Department of Trade and Commerce. There may be some persons who could qualify as scientists who are there employed on certain work that is being done; but we do not know of any employed in that way.
If the minister will allow me to do so, I will return to this question a little later on. In the meantime I will go and get my list because I am afraid I have left it upstairs.
The telephone book.

Yes; that is quite right. I should be happy if the minister would just indicate how many there are. I have no means of knowing that they are experts. They just look, in the list, as though they were experts, and they appear to be called that; but I will revert to this question later.
Has the minister the number of employees on the Lacombe farm?

About 35 people are
employed on the Lacombe farm.
Supply-Agriculture

I should like to ask one question with regard to item 13, on the experimental farms service. This year there is quite a large increase, about half a million dollars, in the central experimental farm estimate. Can the minister give the committee some idea what this is for? I understood him to say a few minutes ago that the total revenue from the experimental farm was some $400,000. That seems to be a small revenue for the wonderful acreage there and the amount it is costing to run that farm. 1 might also say that there is a certain rumour that has been gaining ground here in the city of Ottawa and I have been asked several times about it. I do not know anything about the matter but I happened to be out in that section a few days ago and the rumour was that consideration was being given to removing part of this experimental farm to some other locality. For instance it is said that the locality in which they are situated now is not proper nor has not been found useful for growing certain kinds of fruit. It was thought that part of the farm was going to be moved to another section in order to cultivate berries and fruit of all kinds. I said that I would make inquiries whether there was any truth in this rumour that is going around. Those are a few of my questions to the minister.

In the first place, there is no plan to move anyone so far as we know. There are of course people who would like to see us move someone so that they can get room to do something else they want to do, but we have no plans to move anyone.
On the other question, as to what this additional expenditure is for, it is largely for building and the increases in salaries because of the natural increase which is provided for as civil servants go on serving one year after another. But the fact that the building cost is up this year has something to do with the activities of the gentleman who was spoken of so highly by the hon. member for Souris at the beginning of this discussion. Dr. Archibald has been at the head of the experimental farms staffs for thirty-one years, I think; and during the last four or five years, since the end of the war, he has been advocating the carrying on of building programs at different places, plans which he had laid even before the war and which we delayed until the war was over. Then when the war was over, because we could not get materials we delayed still further. This year when we were discussing our estimates before the treasury board, in view of the fact that Dr. Archibald is coming towards the end of his service. I insisted strongly that he should get

Supply-Agriculture
the credit for this work that he has been developing and which someone is going to do shortly in any case, and that the erection of buildings to provide for activities which he has been building up and advocating over the years ought to be carried on while he is still there; and so we are going ahead with the work this year.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: The minister explained that one of the reasons for the increase in these items had to do with the natural increase in salaries and so on. At the outset I may say that I am not rising, as some of my friends do, with the object of complaining about these increases. I am rising to inquire as to the situation under this item for central experimental farms, inasmuch as over on page 80 it is indicated that part of it was an increase in the wages paid for temporary assistance and part of it was in wages paid to casuals and others. My question is this. Has there been any improvement in the position of carpenters and of manual workers, nonskilled workers and others, about whom the minister and I have had discussions during the last couple of sessions?

There has been a general increase all along the line in connection with what is generally known as casual labour or persons who are employed in the neighbourhood round about these farms. I do not think anyone would call it a big increase. One of the reasons for that is that we find it necessary to keep the pay of those we are engaging upon the experimental farm in reasonable relationship to what farmers are paying in the district round about. If we get out of line, it sometimes makes it difficult for persons who are employing labour in the neighbourhood. That to an extent accounts for the fact that perhaps the pay looks to be lower in some of these cases than it otherwise might be. But nevertheless there has been an increase, although not as much as my hon. friend was asking for a year or so ago. There has been an increase in the rates.

I should now like to ask this question of the minister in somewhat more detail. I have now the list. Would it suit the minister if I just read some of them out? If the men in his department do not know them, it would be nice if they could meet their opposite numbers in the Department of Trade and Commerce. I will just read these out. Of course I cannot tell by looking at the names whether they are

scientists; but as far as possible I have omitted those that are in the export division because the minister did explain about those. I will therefore just read a few that look to me as if they were scientists and the minister can explain what the situation is. This is the agricultural commodities branch:	director,
G.	R. Paterson; commodities section, chief
H.	A. Gilbert; dairy and poultry products, K. L. Melvin; livestock and animal products, D. G. W. Douglas; plants and products, C. F. Clingan. Then I read again later on, under agriculture division, crop section, the chief is W. D. Porter. There are other names which I will not read. Will the minister tell me how this question can best be answered if this is not the best way. It seems to me it would be very desirable for those of us who do not understand these things very well to have it made clear to us why there appears to be this rather wide duplication.

I think I can best illustrate what the meaning of that is by just taking the first name, Mr. Paterson. I met Mr. Paterson first over in London, but I knew from the records of the department that he was first an employee of the agricultural department years ago. Then he went from the Department of Agriculture to the Department of Trade and Commerce because they wanted a man overseas who understood the agricultural position in Canada, so that he might promote the sale of agricultural products over in Britain. Trade and Commerce had him over there for a number of years. The next place 1 met him was down in Washington. He was there up to within the last year. Then he was moved back to Ottawa largely because of the wide experience he has had in the markets in which we are going to sell farm products.
In the first place, he is a practical agriculturist, trained in the Department of Agriculture. Over the years he has been trained in the Department of Trade and Commerce as one advocating the sale of Canadian farm products over in Europe and then down in the United States. He has gained experience there, and the department has brought him back here because he can instruct those who are working here in what is required in those other countries, and in what they ought to be attempting to do in the way of promoting sales. That, in general, is what has happened so far as Mr. Paterson is concerned. I think you will find that that is pretty well true of the others. That is the general practice.
For example, I was over in Britain in 1936, and I started looking around for persons who were promoting the sale of agricultural products. When I came back from Britain I said

to my officials that I met only one man over there in the service who really understood agriculture. They said:	"Where is he?"
I said:	"He is in Glasgow." I told them of
my experience, of how I went to the auction sale ring where they were selling a load of Canadian cattle. I told them that this man seemed to know all about cattle. He seemed to know all about the individuals who wanted to buy cattle in Scotland, and talked to me very intelligently about the whole matter. Well, two of my officials went over to Scotland a month or two later. When they came back one of them came into my office and said:	"You don't seem to be a very good
checker on persons who understand agriculture." I said: "What makes you think that?" He said:	"We were travelling on the train
from Glasgow to Edinburgh and we were naming the different kinds of cattle as we went along, and this fellow said:	"You fellows must be remarkable chaps, that you can tell these cattle at this distance. Apparently he did not know very much about cattle. He could not tell Ayrshires from Holsteins, passing them on a train." After that experience we thought there should be more people in the service who did know agriculture and knew it in detail, because when you get over there talking to individuals with regard to livestock, and particularly in a place like Scotland, you have to know something about them or they will soon find you out. It is important that there be men with practical experience and that they have technical knowledge with regard to agriculture in general in that department if they are to assist in selling our produce in other countries.

Will the
minister say in answer to me that these other names that I read would be in a category similar to that which he has described? In other words, although it is not apparent at first glance, that they are in fact either directly or indirectly engaged in the export trade and in the business of selling our products and that is merely because you have people in agriculture engaged in that business that they are there in the Department of Trade and Commerce. Is that correct?

Yes, that is true, and they do this as well. When persons come over here from Europe who are looking for cattle, let us say, these individuals take them in tow. They bring them over to our department and we get the best experts that we have to go along with them. They go out and visit herds in different parts of the country and select what they want to take back with them. They assist them in that way. It is much better of course to have men
Supply-Agriculture
in that department to meet them firsthand when they come into the office, talk to them and then act as co-ordinators between that department and our own.

What is the total acreage in the central experimental farm in Ottawa, and also the land taken over from the Scott property last year? What additional facilities are being provided at the farm with the additional property taken over?
The farm is about 1,200 acres. I think the price that we paid for the Scott farm was about $68,000. It is used largely for the purpose of experimenting with seed production of different kinds.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: When the minister answered the hon. member for Queens a few minutes ago with regard to the rumours about moving the experimental farm, or even part of it, away from the city he indicated that his department was not doing anything about it, although he said he did understand that some people were anxious to get the farm moved away so that they could do something else there. What had he in mind, the Ottawa city hall that keeps moving around from place to place, or was it a housing development? I myself am not pressing for the moving of the farm, but it does seem to me that a case could be made out for the large acreage being moved out a bit, although I am not in favour of the beautiful park being moved from where it is. In view of the interest in the whole question, it does seem to me that the minister might have commented further on it.
Well, I have been spending the last two years keeping out of that discussion, and I am going to stay right out of it. It is none of my business where they build the city hall.
Keep the farm.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: That is not an answer to my question.

stations, $5,977,447.

I am very proud to announce that we have an experimental substation in our community. If the other substations and experimental farms throughout Canada prove their worth in the same way they certainly are worth all the money that is spent upon them. But it depends upon the superintendent. We have a superintendent who does his work splendidly. The farmers may visit him at any time except Sunday, and sometimes they try to slip in on him then but he is not there.

Supply-Agriculture
You would be surprised what he does on Sundays when you are not there.

He works the substation well, but he helps the school fairs, the rural fairs, and the different clubs like the one hundred bushels to the acre oat club and the five hundred bushels to the acre potato club. I announced earlier in the year the success of the experiment. The expert farmers in the east might learn something from our district. We had fourteen contestants in the potato club of 500 bushels to the acre, and the average was 350. If some of these men, even from the maritimes and from eastern Ontario, think they can grow a crop of potatoes I say that we can teach them something. If you will visit Fort William we will take you out and show you an experimental substation that is doing its work in a splendid way, and which has had 105 bushels to the acre. Not many farmers in the east raise it; yet we do it and I pay tribute to our substation and our superintendent.
How is it that Simcoe county gets a thousand bushels to the acre?

The hon. member for Simcoe North asked the minister a question some time ago, as to why Simcoe county apples are better than those from British Columbia. I am not admitting that they are; but the British Columbia fruit growers sold large quantities of British Columbia apples in Ontario while the Simcoe apples were being offered for sale. At the present time we are taking orders right here in Ottawa for this year's crop.
I should like to make a few remarks about the experimental station at Summerland, which has been doing excellent work throughout the years on behalf of agriculture in the southern interior of British Columbia and even on a wider field than that. Some years ago the staff from the experimental farm during the winter months attended farmers institute meetings, and meetings of fruit growers, and gave lectures. However in recent years that practice has not been followed. I do suggest that where it is possible, and does not interfere with the work of the station, the officials might be made available to farmers institutes and fruit growers organizations, so that they could render a valuable assistance to farmers, particularly during the winter months, by giving them information on the latest method of farming, and as to tests they have been conducting.

Extension work is done largely under the agricultural colleges. We discuss education here from time to time, and we always come to the conclusion that it is

a provincial responsibility. In connection with agriculture, in common with other activities, it has been carried on largely by the provinces. The extension work is from the agricultural colleges and, while our men do go out, they do so on invitation to gatherings of the kinds mentioned. The common practice is for our cereals men to be at the experimental stations at a certain time of the year. People will gather in there from the surrounding community, and the representative will go over the plots with them and indicate the method of planting, pointing out the different rows representing different methods, and what the results have been.

At Summerland there are valuable tests of fruit and vegetable varieties, and the conclusions are published in reports. As many of the farmers do not see those reports, it would be very helpful to the farmers in the interior if occasionally officials could attend farmers meetings during the winter months, and give them a personal report of those tests on certain fruits and vegetables. Personal contact by officials with the farmers is worth a great deal.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: Does the hon. member, the acting leader of the C.C.F., realize what that would add to the travelling allowances the Tory party is fighting about?
We are not fighting about it.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext:
The travelling allowance
would be increased.

Perhaps they could
travel a lot farther on the same allowance.

When my colleagues and I ask for explanations of increases we should not be said by the parliamentary assistant to be complaining. Surely
we are entitled to know what the money is being spent for? In respect of item 15, which deals with branch farms and stations, and illustration stations, would the minister tell us whether his officials in Newfoundland are active in trying to set up illustration stations there? The report of the department for 1949 refers to 203 illustration stations across Canada, throughout the different provinces.
There are parts of Newfoundland in which the people do not practise even the rotation of crops. They plant potatoes in the same plots year after year. I never see any agricultural representative visiting them or telling them about this new scientific service mentioned over the C.B.C. I should like to see some of the officials who understand these things go down there and help our people take advantage of the latest discoveries. Perhaps it might be possible to bring down films showing exactly what can be done in the matter of strip farming, and other agricultural

practices. Is the minister in a position to make a statement in this respect? I know his department has taken over the experimental farm, which was already doing good work, but which did not reach out far enough. Some students were taken in and given training, and then permitted to go away. I am thinking more particularly of the districts of Ferryland and Trepassey. There the people raise cattle, and graze them on pasture and hayland. I believe they have land there that could be developed considerably through proper methods. I should hope that the minister could assist us by having a representative come and look into the matter.
The minister has promised that he will make a visit to the Peace river area and the Alaska highway. Is he going to visit Newfoundland? This is the second year of confederation for us, and we would deem it a great honour to have so distinguished an agriculturist visit us. I would suggest that he come at the end of the growing season so that he would be able to see the kind of produce we have. Perhaps we could entertain him at dinner, using our produce, and giving him an opportunity to compare it with what is produced in other parts of Canada.

As the hon. member knows, on April 1, we took over the experimental farm in Newfoundland. We have taken over the organization that was there, and are adding to it as we think necessary. In addition to that we are preparing to make a soil survey. I do not know that it can be completed in one season, but we are beginning it this year.
A soil survey was made by one of our highest officials. He has been conducting this for several years.

Any information that is there will be utilized, of course. We will go on from that point.	This will lead to the
establishment of experimental stations, because we establish those stations in relation to the nature of the soil in the different areas. My office files indicate that people are writing in almost weekly pointing out that their soil conditions are different from the conditions at some other point-just as the hon. member for Medicine Hat indicated a moment ago that it is all very well to have a station associated with the ranching south of Medicine Hat, but that they want another station associated with irrigation west of Medicine Hat. We receive requests of that kind all the time.
We are not in a position to determine whether we should put in a station until we know the nature of the soil. We do not want to have three or four stations oper-
Supply-Agriculture
ating in the same type of soil. However, all that work will be proceeded with as rapidly as possible. I might add that much of the production service in connection with agriculture has always been carried on by the provinces-and still is. I presume that will be the condition in Newfoundland, as well as in the other provinces.
With regard to my own trip to Newfoundland, may I say I have flown over that province on two or three occasions, and have landed a number of times at the airport. I have never yet flown over the Alaska highway, and that is one reason I am driving it first. However, I hope that as soon as possible after that I will be able to go to Newfoundland. I am pleased to know that it is best to be there in the fall, because I would not find it possible to be there before that. If at all possible I shall come down there later in the season.
We will look forward to seeing you.

Mr. Chairman, with your indulgence and that of the minister perhaps I can eliminate two speeches by commenting on items 16, 17 and 18. I think the minister is apprized of what I am going to say, but before I say it I must compliment the hon. member for Haldimand, the hon. member for Brant and the hon. member from Newfoundland who have opened up these problems that are facing the minister. I am speaking on the administration item so I believe I am thoroughly in order.
When I think of what they have said I think of something else I have observed in the quarter century I have been here. You, Mr. Chairman, are younger than some of the rest of us, and along with others you may think that I have no right to speak about agriculture. I came into this honourable house as the member for York East, which was a farming constituency. I lived on lot 30 of a concession of East Scarborough where I was carrying on my occupation as an agriculturist. A quarter of a century is not a very long time to go back.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: Hear, hear.

I think I have a perfect right to talk about agriculture as I may know something about it, with all respect to the "hear, hear." If I can add anything to these deliberations I have the right to do so because wherefrom came my bread came my livelihood, and wherefrom came my livelihood came my tenure of office in this assembly. I

Supply-Agriculture
should like to make a few observations of a general nature and then deal particularly with items 16, 17 and 18.
In the quarter of a century I have been sitting here I have seen how different governments operate and I have seen how ministers dominate the entire situation as far as the estimates are concerned. I may not be here very long but I ask those charged with the administration of the departments to allow the deputies or the deputies' deputies to pay attention to the humble remarks which hon. members on all sides of this chamber put on Hansard and reply to them in one way or another. Some machinery should be set up so that the minister would not have to answer every two-cent question we ask.
Some way should be found whereby the plethora of men, women and children in your department who are drawing big pay should toe able to discuss these matters with the members and answer some of the questions that are asked from all sides of the House of Commons. In my opinion, those in the department have some knowledge of departmental matters. If they do not have that knowledge they should not be within the confines of the department and drawing the pay which we extract from the taxpayers of Canada.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: Hear, hear.

I speak with the voice of experience because I have asked questions for a quarter of a century. I am ashamed to say in this chamber tonight that it is my experience that while I have presented a simple problem, while I have placed my questions on Hansard, never yet have I got an answer. I do not want it from the minister who is away up in a seventh heaven; I just want a simple answer such as a farmer from the constituency of York East would expect. But 1 have not got it. Yet you and I and the rest of us in this honourable chamber think that we are working for democracy.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: Hear, hear.

Never mind the "hear, hear". I think it is the loud voice of mine that is getting an echo. It is very hard for me to hear. If for a moment I may go to some other sea-I think the hon. member comes from near the sea.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: That is right.
Or away out the other way.
He is the margarine branch.

The margarine
branch. When the Angel Gabriel comes

down to this earth and puts one foot on part of British Columbia and the other out in the Pacific ocean and proclaims that earth shall be no more, my hon. friend from British Columbia will rise in his place and say, "Hear, hear."
If I may now get back to the subject I rose to speak about as quietly as possible, I think our democracy would extend its democratic tendencies if attention were paid to what appears in Hansard, and to what is said by members like myself. We are not highly educated, we may not be Rhodes scholars and know how to use language, but generally we know what we are talking about. We use plain English. The minister has to toil twenty hours a day as some of us did in our youth in order to gain a footing in this world. He has a great deputy alongside him, who in turn has other deputies, and it should be possible for them to reply to simple questions asked by hon. members on all sides of the house so that they may realize that they are working in a democracy.
Ninety-nine times out of one hundred you and your deputies will be right because we are an innocent-minded sort of people. But neither the minister nor his deputy has answered the question which I asked a year ago. I doubt if one bit of attention was ever paid to what I said, or if there was I never heard of it. I have reiterated these statements time after time because if they were worked out they would add a million dollars to the economy of this country. There are enough idlers in the research branch to do what I would like to see done.
I do not think you said this on our estimates last year.

I know what I am talking about. When I was young it was not just a case of taking a bear off a Ford car. I was dealing with boars with two big tusks and other appendages that were not at all necessary. I bought them for $5 apiece and sold them for $40. That is the way I made my election expenses in 1921 to the extent of nearly $20,000.
It was not worth it.

I want to improve
the economy of this country if I can and attention should be paid to ideas that emanate-from members of this House of Commons regardless of their politics. We are not politicians. We are here because we have a job to do for Canada. At the present time of necessity the minister must handle everything with his own hands, but there are able men and women in his department who could work out these different problems and answer

these different questions. Among the problems which I have recited to him before-and I never will again because I may never be here again-is the problem of waste. Every time you feed 100,000 people you have enough waste left over to feed 10,000 hogs. When I realize that 10,000 hogs will gain at least a pound a day, as some members know, and most of them a pound and a quarter, when I realize that hogs are worth 30 cents a pound, I also realize what we could do for the economy of Canada if that one little bit of waste could be avoided. One and all should read the speech made by Lloyd George in 1911 about the waste in the United Kingdom at that time and try to visualize that compared with the waste of all kinds that is going on in Canada now. It is not waste entirely because I sat in the Chateau last night, paid $5 for $2 worth of food and saw the "waists" around there. It reminds me not only of the waste that Lloyd George referred to, not only of the waste that is going on in Canada all the time, but of the waste of our talents, efforts and energies in this Canada of ours.
I should like to ask the minister if same sort of research could not be instituted to take care of the change in the trend of the feeding of waste to hogs because of the advent, as I mentioned a few years ago-and I hope I never have occasion to mention it again-of the soap operators and the increased production of alkali soaps and cleansers such as Spic and Span and so on. All these things eventually find their way into the swill can and from there into the production of millions of pounds of pork in Canada. There is one pound of this stuff in every hundred pounds and it finds its way into the organs of the hog which is affected by it. That in turn is destroying the economy of Canada to the extent of many hundreds of thousands of dollars, and it could be very easily taken care of under the vote which we are considering now. Some thought should be given to the feeders of hogs outside the large municipalities. There is one just two miles from where we are sitting who picks up the garbage from the restaurant. I hope there is not too much alkali in it and that they are not poisoning the hogs. They disturb the inner activities of the hog.
I run a hospital but I am not a doctor. If I were I could tell you exactly how they are disturbing the inner workings of the hog. The hog gets swine fever and not cholera. The minister and his deputy think only of cholera coming from some foreign source but it is swine fever. I know because that is how I earn my living. If they could have one of the men in their research department spend some of his time to clear up this matter and neutralize the effect of the alkali feeds that are
Supply-Agriculture
finding their way into hog production then they might be doing something on behalf of the economy of Canada and for those of us who make a few dollars out of this particular vocation. They might be doing something for us but I am thinking more particularly of the general economy of Canada. I appreciate that the minister may not be a pig man and that perhaps other things are of more interest to him. Nevertheless here is one portion of our economy to which one of his thousand servants might at least give some attention, and which would work out in due course in my opinion to the general advantage of Canada.

Item agreed to.
IS. Compensation for animals slaughtered, $1,091,292.
Under the amended Animal Contagious Diseases Act, what was the amount of compensation paid in Brant, Oxford, Middlesex and Elgin counties last year?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Agriculture
speechtext: If I understood the question of the hon. member for Brant-Wentworth, he wants to know the amount of compensation paid in Brant and Oxford counties?
And also Middlesex and Elgin.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Agriculture
speechtext: I think there was a realm made for the counties of Oxford and Elgin but Brant and Middlesex were not given. We have not that information now. It will take us about twenty-four hours to get it, but if the hon. member wants if we will secure it for Brant and Middlesex and give it to him.
Perhaps the minister might make a two minute reply to my twenty minute diatribe.

The hon. member has had a lot of hogs fed and no doubt has fed a lot of them, and for that reason he will know that we must keep a check on the feeding of hogs that are fed in the manner he was describing, namely, from cooked garbage. There are 601 such licensed feeders in Canada and right now they are feeding 53,565 hogs. Therefore it is not a part of the industry that is not flourishing. It is carrying on at present time and is under supervision of officials of the department.
It will soon cease if you do not take care of it.

I do not know whether I have answered your question. I think it is true that we have as good a record, and probably the best record, with regard to cholera and other hog diseases as any other place in the world.

Supply-Agriculture
Make sure that the alkalinity and acidity are carefully checked as to these 53,000 hogs.
The only thing I can say is that the losses are not great.
Don't wait for losses.

I do not altogether understand the remarks of the hon. member. He has been here for twenty-five years and I have been here for fifteen. I do not think that in that fifteen years he has ever asked me a straight question to which he has not received a straight answer. I have not taken the same liberties with him that I take with some others for certain reasons, and particularly when he is talking about hogs and the feeding of hogs, because I know he knows what he is talking about. I also know he is not trying to put in a little time. Therefore I have always undertaken to answer him when he has asked me questions.
Will you promise us some research?
We are at it all the time, and the very fact that we have the lowest amount of disease from that kind of thing of any country in the world is the answer.

That is not the
answer.
I do not say it is all due to what we do.	*
It is due to cold weather and God's good grace.
It is also due to the efforts of feeders like yourself.
Can the minister say how many new t.b. free areas were established in Alberta last year?
I understand that eight or ten were started but only one was completed.

Is it the intention of the federal government to proceed with that work? I believe only a small portion of the province is organized at the present time. I remember that some years ago a district was formed and it was said to be the intention of the federal government to expand the area as rapidly as possible. Then the war came along, of course, and the work was stopped. Is it the intention to proceed fairly rapidly with the expansion of these areas?

We are proceeding as rapidly as we can obtain the men to do the work. As I said last session and the session before, we have not limited this work by keeping down the cost. We have been voting all the

money we could profitably expend, and it is purely a matter of getting a sufficient number of veterinarians to do the work. As far as Alberta is concerned, as my hon. friend knows it was the last province to permit us to come in and do this work. The ranchers were absolutely opposed to it. It is only since I have been in Ottawa-and I have been here fifteen years-that this work has been commenced in Alberta. We have been carrying on there as rapidly as possible, but the service has not gone ahead in Alberta, because of that fact, as rapidly as in other provinces.
Approximately what percentage of the cattle population of Canada have been tested?
About 63 per cent of the cattle.

If the minister would permit me to go back to item No. 17 for just a moment, I see that the number of veterinarians is somewhere near what it was before the war. I wonder if the minister knows how many graduates will be coming into the permanent service from the Ontario and Quebec veterinary colleges this year.
We expect about thirty new appointments this year.
To the permanent staff?
Yes.

Could the minister tell
us when we may expect the time to be shortened between the application and the actual testing? At present it takes almost a year from the time the application is made until the herd is tested, and many of our farmers who have made application to have their herd accredited would like to have it done much sooner. Can the minister say when that position might be cleared up?

Well, a year seems quite a long time, but if it is that long it is because of what I just stated. We have difficulty in getting enough veterinarians to do all the work that has to be done, not only in districts but in the testing of accredited herds.

Item agreed to.
19. Livestock and poultry, $1,342,738.

This is the item under which the minister said he would explain the steps that have been taken to control Newcastle disease on Vancouver island. I have had reports of new cases discovered as recently as June 6. I am particularly anxious to know not only what is being done, but whether the department has enough veterinarians in that district to control the disease, and also

whether tests have been made with the vaccines used in the United States, I believe with a considerable degree of success.

Perhaps the best answer I can give with regard to Newcastle disease on the coast is to merely recite the figures. The flocks under slaughter order numbered 201 as of June 10. Up to that date the destroyed flocks numbered 194 and the birds destroyed totalled 307,217. The eggs destroyed in fully reported destroyed flocks numbered 202,140. The compensation awarded in fully reported destroyed flocks was $421,357.83; and the officials in charge think they have it under control. I believe that is the most complete answer I can give my hon. friend.
Is it possible to import, into British Columbia and use on the flocks there the vaccine which has been tried in Washington with success, as I am informed?

The department is satisfied that the vaccination which has been found successful in some areas south of the line no doubt will be utilized in this country at a later stage in fighting the disease, but it is felt that at present the most important thing is to slaughter the herds and get rid of them entirely, and also get rid of the eggs produced by the flocks. When the matter is fully under control the question of vaccination in order to prevent the disease from infecting flocks elsewhere may be considered, but at the present time it is felt advisable to go on with the slaughter of flocks, paying for those destroyed.
The vaccine cannot be imported now, I believe; is that right?

There are two vaccines, one known as dead vaccine and the other as live vaccine. It is not permitted to import the live vaccine from the United States, but the dead vaccine is produced here in our own laboratories. Up to the present time the importation of live vaccine has been prohibited because under those circumstances it does spread the disease.

Out in our
part of the country the provincial governments are attempting to control Bang's disease. Is the federal government giving any assistance, or is there any federal program to eliminate this disease or prevent it from spreading?
The federal government cooperates with the provinces. We provide the vaccine and the province applies it.

I wonder if the minister can tell us how many reactors there were among the cattle tested in Prince Edward Island?
